Medically reviewed by Carmen Pope, Senior Medical Editor, B. Pharm .
Last updated on Aug 27, 2026.
Adderall (mixed amphetamine and dextroamphetamine salts) is a central nervous system stimulant used to treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and a sleep disorder called narcolepsy.
Adderall contains a combination of amphetamine and dextroamphetamine, which affect chemicals in the brain and nerves that contribute to hyperactivity and impulse control.
For ADHD, Adderall is used in children 3 to 17 years of age and in adults.
It may help increase attention and decrease impulsiveness and hyperactivity.
For narcolepsy, Adderall is used in people 6 years and older.
It is not known if Adderall is safe and effective for ADHD in children under 3 years of age or for narcolepsy in children under 6 years of age.
Adderall is a federally controlled substance (CII) because it contains amphetamine, which can be a target for people who abuse prescription medicines or street drugs.
Keep Adderall in a safe place to protect it from theft.
Never give your Adderall to anyone else, because it may cause death or harm them.
Selling or giving away Adderall is against the law.
Adderall may also be used for purposes not listed in this medication guide.
Adderall (mixed amphetamine and dextroamphetamine salts) was FDA-approved on January 19, 1960.
Extended-release formulations of Adderall ( Adderall XR ) are only used to treat ADHD.
Adderall has a Boxed Warning for abuse, misuse, and addiction.
Adderall has a high chance of abuse and misuse and may lead to substance use problems, including addiction.
Misuse and abuse of Adderall, other amphetamine-containing medicines, and methylphenidate-containing medicines can lead to overdose and death.
The risk of overdose and death is increased with higher doses or when the medicine is used in ways that are not approved, such as snorting or injection.
Adderall may lead to physical dependence after prolonged use, even if taken as directed.
Your healthcare provider should check you or your child for the risk of abuse, misuse, and addiction before starting treatment and will monitor you or your child during treatment.
Tell your healthcare provider if you or your child has ever abused or been dependent on alcohol, prescription medicines, or street drugs.
Stimulants have caused stroke, heart attack, and sudden death in people with high blood pressure, heart disease, or a heart defect.
Your healthcare provider should check you or your child carefully for heart problems before starting Adderall and should check blood pressure and heart rate regularly during treatment.

Call your healthcare provider right away or go to the nearest hospital emergency room if you or your child have any signs of heart problems, such as chest pain, shortness of breath, or fainting during treatment.

Adderall may cause new or worse behavior and thought problems, new or worse bipolar illness, or new psychotic symptoms (such as hearing voices, or seeing or believing things that are not real) or new manic symptoms.
This is more likely if you have a history of depression, mental illness, or bipolar disorder.
Tell your healthcare provider about any mental problems you or your child have, or about a family history of suicide, bipolar illness, or depression.

Call your healthcare provider right away if you or your child have any new or worsening mental symptoms during treatment, especially hearing voices, seeing or believing things that are not real, or new manic symptoms.
You may have blood circulation problems that can cause numbness, pain, or discoloration in your fingers or toes.
Call your doctor right away if you have unexplained wounds appearing on your fingers or toes during treatment.

Do not use Adderall if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days, such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine, or if you have received a methylene blue injection.
A dangerous drug interaction could occur.

You may not be able to use Adderall if you have glaucoma, an overactive thyroid, severe anxiety or agitation, moderate to severe high blood pressure, heart disease or coronary artery disease, vascular disease, or a history of drug or alcohol addiction.
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to Adderall: hives, difficult breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Adderall may cause serious side effects.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
signs of heart problems, such as chest pain, trouble breathing, or feeling like you might pass out
signs of psychosis, such as hallucinations, new behavior problems, aggression, hostility, or paranoia
signs of circulation problems, such as numbness, pain, a cold feeling, unexplained wounds, or skin color changes (pale, red, or blue appearance) in your fingers or toes
a seizure
muscle twitches (tics)
changes in your vision.
See warnings above.
Children should have their height and weight checked often during treatment, and your healthcare provider may stop treatment if your child is not growing or gaining weight as expected.
This problem may happen when Adderall is taken with certain other medicines and may be life-threatening.

Stop taking Adderall and get medical help right away if you develop agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Common side effects of Adderall may include stomach pain, loss of appetite, weight loss, mood changes, feeling nervous, fast heart rate, headache, dizziness, sleep problems (insomnia), and dry mouth.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Do not take Adderall if you or your child:
are allergic to amphetamine products or any of the ingredients in Adderall (see ingredients below)
are taking, or have taken within the past 14 days, an MAO inhibitor, including the antibiotic linezolid or the intravenous medicine methylene blue.
have a rare adrenal gland tumor called pheochromocytoma.
Before taking Adderall, tell your healthcare provider about all your medical conditions including if you or anyone in your family has ever had:
heart problems, heart disease, heart defects, or high blood pressure, or a family history of sudden death or heart problems
mental problems including psychosis, mania, bipolar illness, or depression, or a family history of suicide, bipolar illness, or depression
kidney or liver problems
seizures or an abnormal brain wave test (EEG)
circulation problems in the fingers or toes
repeated movements or sounds (tics) or Tourette's syndrome, or a family history of tics or Tourette's syndrome.
Also tell your doctor if you are pregnant, intending to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.
Taking Adderall during pregnancy can cause premature birth, low birth weight, or withdrawal symptoms in the newborn baby.
Tell your healthcare provider if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
There is a pregnancy registry that collects information about the health of females exposed to Adderall and their babies.
Adderall passes into breast milk and may harm a nursing baby.
You should not breastfeed during treatment with Adderall.
Talk to your healthcare provider about the best way to feed the baby during treatment.
Take Adderall exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider.
Follow all directions on your prescription label.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Do not take this medicine in larger or smaller amounts or for longer than recommended.
The first dose of the day is usually taken when you first wake up .
Taking this medicine in the afternoon may cause trouble sleeping.
Adderall can be taken with or without food.
Do not crush or chew an extended-release capsule.
Swallow it whole.
To make swallowing easier, you may open the capsule and sprinkle the medicine into a spoonful of applesauce, then swallow all of the mixture right away without chewing.
Do not divide the medicine in the capsule, and do not save the mixture for later use.
Adderall may be habit-forming.
Never share this medicine with another person, especially someone with a history of drug abuse or addiction.
Keep the medicine where others cannot get to it.
While using this medicine, your doctor will need to check your progress at regular visits.
Adderall can cause unusual results with certain medical tests, so tell any doctor who treats you that you are using this medicine.
Your healthcare provider may tell you to stop taking this medicine for a short time before you get certain imaging tests.

Initial dose: 5 mg orally 1 or 2 times a day.
Maintenance dose: the daily dose may be raised in 5 mg increments at weekly intervals until an optimal response is obtained.
Maximum dose: only in rare cases will it be necessary to exceed 40 mg per day.

Initial dose: 5 or 10 mg orally once a day in the morning.
Maintenance dose: the daily dose may be raised in 5 to 10 mg increments at weekly intervals.

Initial dose: 10 mg orally once a day.

Initial dose: 5 mg orally per day in divided doses.
Maintenance dose: the daily dose may be raised in 5 mg increments at weekly intervals until an optimal response is obtained.
Immediate-release (IR) , ages 12 years and older:
Initial dose: 10 mg orally per day in divided doses.
Maintenance dose: the daily dose may be raised in 10 mg increments at weekly intervals until an optimal response is obtained.
Narcolepsy rarely occurs in children under 12 years of age.

If you or your child takes too much Adderall, call your healthcare provider or the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222, or go to the nearest hospital emergency room right away.
An overdose of Adderall could be fatal.
Overdose symptoms may include restlessness, tremor, muscle twitches, rapid breathing, confusion, hallucinations, panic, aggressiveness, muscle pain or weakness, and dark colored urine.
These symptoms may be followed by depression and tiredness.
Other symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, uneven heartbeats, feeling light-headed, fainting, seizure, or coma.
This medicine may impair your thinking or reactions.
Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be alert.
Avoid drinking fruit juices or taking vitamin C at the same time you take Adderall.
These can make your body absorb less of the medicine.

The primary difference between Adderall and Vyvanse lies in their composition: Adderall contains a mixture of four different amphetamine salts, while Vyvanse contains only one type of amphetamine salt called lisdexamfetamine.
Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) is a prodrug that converts into dexamphetamine once absorbed by the body.
Adderall's four amphetamine salts include dextroamphetamine saccharate, amphetamine aspartate, dextroamphetamine sulfate, and amphetamine sulfate.
People taking Adderall for ADHD typically notice improved focus and attention and reduced impulsivity.
In people without ADHD, it can also enhance focus, alertness, and energy levels.
When taken as prescribed, the effects of Adderall last for about 4 to 6 hours.
The effects of Adderall XR last for up to 12 hours because this brand of Adderall is designed for slow and sustained release.
Continue reading
Modafinil and Adderall are both classified as CNS stimulants but have different chemical structures, which means there are differences in their addiction potential and risk of side effects.
Modafinil and Adderall both have stimulant-type effects, but modafinil is a much milder stimulant than Adderall.
Focalin contains dexmethylphenidate whereas Adderall contains a mixture of amphetamine salts (MAS).

Both have a high potential for abuse and dependence, although the risk may be perceived as higher with Adderall because it is more popular; however, this does not mean Focalin is less likely to cause tolerance or dependence.

It is difficult to say exactly how long Adderall withdrawal lasts because it depends on the person and the process is different for everyone.
Some people’s withdrawal symptoms may resolve in as little as 5 days, others may still be experiencing symptoms 4 weeks later or even longer.
People who have taken Adderall for a long time at a high dose should expect withdrawal symptoms to last longer, sometimes several months.
Continue reading
Adderall tongue is a common side effect of Adderall that can detrimentally and seriously affect a person’s quality of life.
To help relieve Adderall tongue stay well-hydrated.
Adderall and other ADHD medications can cause dehydration, so you need to drink at least 6 to 8 glasses of fluid per day.
Take frequent sips of water rather than drinking a whole glass of water at once.
Use artificial saliva products (such as sprays or lozenges) – these can help moisten the tissue and last longer than water.
There are many different brands of these available over the counter at drug stores and they can be used multiple times a day.
Chew sugar-free gum or suck on sugar-free candy – this contains xylitol which increases salivary flow and can help prevent dental decay.
Avoid sucking candy that contains sugar because this will increase your risk of dental decay Continue reading

Although Adderall is only FDA-approved for the treatment of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy, it has been used rarely and off-label to treat depression that has not responded to other treatments.
However, this is controversial and there is a lack of good quality evidence to support its use.
There is no evidence that Adderall helps with anxiety and in many people with pre-existing mood disorders, Adderall can make depression and/or anxiety worse.

Pronunciation: al-BYOO-ter-all Generic name: albuterol inhalation Brand names: ProAir HFA , ProAir RespiClick , Proventil HFA , Ventolin HFA , AccuNeb (discontinued) Drug class: Adrenergic bronchodilators
Medically reviewed by Philip Thornton, DipPharm .
Last updated on Aug 27, 2026.
Albuterol is a bronchodilator that relaxes muscles in the airways and increases air flow to the lungs.
Albuterol inhalation is used to treat or prevent bronchospasm, or narrowing of the airways in the lungs, in people with asthma or certain types of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
It is also used to prevent exercise-induced bronchospasm.
Albuterol inhalation is for use in adults and children who are at least 2 years old.
Always follow your doctor's directions when giving albuterol to a child.
It is important to keep albuterol on hand at all times.
Get your prescription refilled before you run out of medicine completely.
Keep using all of your other medications as prescribed by your doctor.
Talk with your doctor if any of your asthma medications do not seem to work as well in treating or preventing attacks.
If it seems like you need to use more of any of your medications in a 24-hour period, talk with your doctor.
An increased need for medication could be an early sign of a serious asthma attack.
Only use albuterol as prescribed by your physician.
An overdose of albuterol can be fatal.
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
You should not use this medicine if you are allergic to albuterol.
You should not use ProAir RespiClick or ProAir Digihaler if you are allergic to milk proteins.
To make sure albuterol inhalation is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have:
heart disease, high blood pressure, congestive heart failure;
heart disease, high blood pressure, congestive heart failure;
a heart rhythm disorder;
a heart rhythm disorder;
a seizure disorder such as epilepsy;
a seizure disorder such as epilepsy;
diabetes;
diabetes;
overactive thyroid; or
overactive thyroid; or
low levels of potassium in your blood.
low levels of potassium in your blood.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
It is not known whether albuterol will harm an unborn baby.

However, having uncontrolled asthma during pregnancy may increase the risk of premature birth, low birth weight, or eclampsia (dangerously high blood pressure that can lead to medical problems in both mother and baby).
The benefit of preventing bronchospasm may outweigh any risks to the baby.
If you are pregnant, your name may be listed on a pregnancy registry to track the effects of albuterol on the baby.
It may not be safe to breastfeed while using this medicine.
Ask your doctor about any risk.

Allopurinol belongs to a class of medications called xanthine oxidase inhibitors.
It works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body.
High levels of uric acid may cause gout attacks or kidney stones.

Allopurinol is used to treat gout (a type of arthritis in which uric acid, a naturally occurring substance in the body, builds up in the joints and causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat in one or more joints).
Allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks, not to treat them once they occur.
Allopurinol does not need to be stopped during an acute flare.
Allopurinol is also used to treat high levels of uric acid that builds up in the blood as tumors break down in people with certain types of cancer who are being treated with chemotherapy medications.
It is also used to treat kidney stones that have come back in people who have high levels of uric acid in their urine.
You should not use this medicine if you have ever had an allergic reaction to allopurinol.
Allopurinol can lower blood cells that help your body fight infections.
This can make it easier for you to bleed from an injury or get sick from being around others who are ill.
Your blood may need to be tested often.
Visit your doctor regularly.
In rare cases, allopurinol may cause a severe allergic reaction.

Stop taking this medicine and call your doctor right away if you have painful urination, blood in your urine, burning in your eyes, swelling in your face or throat, skin redness or a rash that spreads and causes blistering and peeling.
Avoid drinking alcohol.

Allopurinol may impair your thinking or reactions.

Amlodipine besylate is a prescription medicine used to treat high blood pressure ( hypertension ) and to prevent certain types of angina ( chest pain ).
It belongs to a class of medications called calcium channel blockers.
Amlodipine besylate works by relaxing and widening the blood vessels, so blood flows more easily which improves blood pressure.
Amlodipine besylate controls angina chest pain by increasing the supply of blood to the heart.
If taken regularly, this medicine controls chest pain, but it does not stop chest pain once it starts.
Your doctor may prescribe a different medication to take when you have chest pain.
Amlodipine is also used alone or in combination with other medicines to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) in adults and children at least 6 years old.
Lowering blood pressure may lower your risk of a stroke or heart attack .

Amlodipine decreases blood pressure over 4 to 8 hours after a single dose.
Because the decrease in blood pressure is gradual, a patient's heart rate is not affected because their physiological reflexes (such as an increase in heart rate) are not activated.
Swelling from amlodipine is a common, but often troublesome side effect of amlodipine with 5% to 9% of people stopping amlodipine because of it.
If you develop swelling with amlodipine, tell your doctor right away because they may be able to change your blood pressure medications slightly to help reduce the swelling.

Swelling caused by amlodipine does not usually respond to treatment with diuretics (such as furosemide) because it is caused by changes in capillary pressure that result in leakage into the spaces between capillaries (called the interstitial area) rather than water retention.
Continue reading
You can take amlodipine in the morning or at night, whichever works best for your schedule.
The key is to take it at the same time each day to maintain consistent blood levels and support its effectiveness.
Amlodipine can stay in your system for up to 11.5 days after your last dose.
This is because it has a long elimination half-life of 30 to 50 hours, meaning it takes that long for your body to reduce the drug level by half.
Weight gain has been reported by some people taking amlodipine but this is not a common side effect and some people have also reported weight loss.
Weight gain with amlodipine may also be a symptom of edema, which is when you retain fluid, which may be particularly noticeable around your ankles or lower legs.
The risk of edema is greater in women compared with men and in those people taking a higher dosage of amlodipine, and edema is usually noticed as weight gain.

Atorvastatin is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of heart attack, stroke, angina, and to decrease the chance that heart surgery will be needed in people who have heart disease or who are at risk of developing heart disease.
Atorvastatin helps lower LDL cholesterol ('bad cholesterol') and triglyceride levels, and increases HDL cholesterol ('good cholesterol') levels, to improve your overall lipid profile.
Atorvastatin calcium belongs to a class of medications called HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, commonly referred to as statins.
Atrovastatin tablets are taken once daily with or without food.
Atorvastatin works by selectively blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the key enzyme the liver uses to produce cholesterol.
By slowing this process, it reduces cholesterol production in the liver and increases the number of LDL receptors on liver cells, which helps remove more LDL (“bad”) cholesterol from the bloodstream.
As a result, it lowers overall LDL levels, decreases the number of LDL particles, and improves the body’s ability to clear cholesterol.
Atorvastatin FDA-approved uses:
To reduce the risk of cardiovascular events in adults with:
Multiple risk factors for coronary heart disease (CHD), but without established CHD.
Use: to reduce the risk of myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, revascularization procedures, and angina.
Type 2 diabetes and multiple risk factors for CHD , without established CHD Use: to help reduce the risk of MI and stroke.
Adults with clinically evident CHD : Use: To reduce the risk of non-fatal MI, fatal and non-fatal stroke, revascularization procedures, hospitalization for congestive heart failure, and angina.
As an adjunct to diet to lower LDL-C:
Adults with primary hyperlipidemia.
Adults and pediatric patients (10 years and older) with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH).
As an adjunct to other LDL-lowering therapies:
For adults and pediatric patients (10 years and older) with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.
As an adjunct to diet for additional lipid disorders in adults:
Primary dysbetalipoproteinemia.
Hypertriglyceridemia.

Rosuvastatin (Crestor) and atorvastatin (Lipitor) are both statins that lower “bad” LDL cholesterol and reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke in people at increased cardiovascular risk.
The better choice for you depends on factors such as how much LDL reduction you need, your medical history, and cost and insurance coverage.
Continue reading
Atorvastatin (also known as Lipitor) can be taken any time of the day, with or without food.
An oral dose of atorvastatin will be absorbed rapidly, with maximum plasma concentrations occurring within 1 to 2 hours after you take it.
While you may or may not eat food when taking atorvastatin, there are certain foods you should avoid when taking the drug.
It takes about 77 hours (3 days) for atorvastatin to be out of your system.
The elimination half life of atorvastatin is approximately 14 hours.
This is the time it takes for your body to reduce plasma drug levels by half.
It takes approximately 5.5 x elimination half lives for a medicine to be out of ones system.

Atorvastatin itself does not consistently cause weight gain in clinical trials, but some studies suggest a small association between statin use (including atorvastatin) and modest weight gain and higher diabetes risk over time.
For most people, the heart‑protective benefits of atorvastatin outweigh these potential metabolic effects, especially when combined with lifestyle measures that support a healthy weight.

Limes, pomegranates, pomelos, and Seville oranges can also interact with some medications, including statins such as atorvastatin.
There just hasn't been as much research published regarding how other types of citrus (apart from grapefruit) interact with statins.
Large quantities of lime or lime peel should be avoided, although small amounts (such as a twist of lime in a drink) are unlikely to cause a significant interaction.

Pronunciation: byoo-PRO-pee-on Generic name: bupropion Brand names: Wellbutrin (discontinued), Wellbutrin SR , Wellbutrin XL , Zyban (discontinued), Aplenzin , Budeprion XL (discontinued), Forfivo XL Drug classes: Miscellaneous antidepressants , Smoking cessation agents
Medically reviewed by Melisa Puckey, BPharm .
Last updated on Sep 10, 2026.
Bupropion is an antidepressant medication used to treat depression and seasonal affective disorder .
It also supports smoking cessation and weight management.
Bupropion is the active ingredient in Wellbutrin and Zyban, Auvelity contains bupropion and dextromethorphan, and Contrave contains bupropion and naltrexone.
Bupropion improves mood regulation and nicotine cravings and, when combined with naltrexone, helps reduce food intake.
Bupropion is thought to work by changing levels of certain chemicals in the brain, including noradrenaline and dopamine.
Bupropion first became an FDA-approved medicine on 30 December 1985.

Get emergency medical help if you have any of these signs of an allergic reaction to bupropion: (hives, itching, fever, swollen glands, difficult breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling).

Report any new or worsening symptoms to your doctor, such as: mood or behavior changes, anxiety, depression, panic attacks, trouble sleeping, or if you feel impulsive, irritable, agitated, hostile, aggressive, restless, hyperactive (mentally or physically), more depressed, or have thoughts about suicide or hurting yourself.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
a seizure (convulsions);
confusion, unusual changes in mood or behavior;
blurred vision, tunnel vision, eye pain or swelling, or seeing halos around lights;
fast or irregular heartbeats; or
a manic episode - racing thoughts, increased energy, reckless behavior, feeling extremely happy or irritable, talking more than usual, severe problems with sleep.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
You should not take bupropion if you have seizures, an eating disorder, or suddenly stopped using alcohol, seizure medication, or sedatives.
You should not take two medicines together that contain bupropion for example, if you take Wellbutrin for depression, you should not also take Contrave for weight control or Aplenzin for depression.

Do not use bupropion within 14 days before or 14 days after you have used a MAO inhibitors , such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine.
Some young people (up to 24 years of age) have thoughts about suicide when first taking this medicine.
Stay alert to changes in your mood or symptoms.
Report any new or worsening symptoms to your doctor.

You should know that your mental health may change in unexpected ways when you take bupropion or other antidepressants even if you are an adult over age 24 or if you do not have a mental illness and you are taking bupropion to treat a different type of condition.
You may become suicidal, especially at the beginning of your treatment and any time that your dose is increased or decreased.

You, your family, or your caregiver should call your doctor right away if you experience any of the following symptoms: new or worsening depression; thinking about harming or killing yourself, or planning or trying to do so; extreme worry; agitation; panic attacks; difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep; aggressive behavior; irritability; acting without thinking; severe restlessness; and frenzied abnormal excitement.
Be sure that your family or caregiver knows which symptoms may be serious so they can call the doctor if you are unable to seek treatment on your own.
This medicine may cause seizures, especially in people with certain medical conditions or when using certain drugs.
Tell your doctor about all of your medical conditions and the drugs you use.
Bupropion can cause mild pupillary dilation, which can lead to an episode of angle-closure glaucoma in susceptible individuals.
Angle-closure glaucoma has occurred in patients with untreated anatomically narrow angles treated with antidepressants.
Do not use this medicine if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days.
A dangerous drug interaction could occur.
MAO inhibitors include isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, tranylcypromine, and others.
You should not take this medicine if you are allergic to it or if you have ever had:
a seizure disorder;
an eating disorder such as anorexia or bulimia; or
if you have suddenly stopped using alcohol, seizure medication, or a sedative (such as Xanax, Valium, Fiorinal, Klonopin, and others).
Do not take this medicine to treat more than one condition at a time.
If you take bupropion for depression, do not also take this medicine to quit smoking or for weight management.
Tell your doctor about all of your medical conditions and the drugs you use.
To make sure this medicine is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
a head injury, seizures, or brain or spinal cord tumor;
narrow-angle glaucoma;
heart disease, high blood pressure, or a heart attack;
diabetes;
kidney or liver disease (especially cirrhosis);
depression, bipolar disorder or other mental illness; or
if you drink alcohol.
Some young people have thoughts about suicide when first taking an antidepressant.
Your doctor will need to check your progress at regular visits while you are using this medicine.
Your family or other caregivers should also be alert to changes in your mood or symptoms.
Talk to your healthcare provider if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant about the risk to your unborn baby.
It is not known whether this medicine will harm an unborn baby.
Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant.
Do not start or stop taking bupropion without your doctor's advice.
If you become pregnant during treatment, talk to your healthcare provider about registering with the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants.
You can register by calling 1-844-405-6185.
Tell your healthcare provider if you are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed while taking this medicine.
This medicine passes into breast milk, and there have been reports of seizures in breastfed infants.
Talk to your healthcare provider about the best way to feed your baby during treatment with this medicine.
Take bupropion exactly as prescribed by your doctor.
Follow all directions on your prescription label.
Do not take this medicine in larger or smaller amounts or for longer than recommended.
Too much of this medicine can increase your risk of a seizure.
Do not crush, chew, or break tablets.
Swallow the tablet whole.
Take bupropion with food if the medication upsets your stomach.
If you have trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, do not take tablets too close to bedtime.
Your doctor will probably start you on a low dose of this medicine and gradually increase your dose.
It may take 4 weeks or longer before you feel the full benefit of this medicine.
Continue to take your tablets even if you feel well.
Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor.
Your doctor may decrease your dose gradually.
You should not change your dose or stop using bupropion suddenly unless you have a seizure while taking this medicine.
Stopping suddenly can cause unpleasant withdrawal symptoms.
Ask your doctor how to stop using bupropion safely.
Some people taking bupropion have severe high blood pressure, especially when using a nicotine replacement product (patch or gum).
Your blood pressure may need to be checked before and during treatment with this medicine.
This medicine can cause you to have a false positive drug screening test ( amphetamines).
If you provide a urine sample for drug screening, tell the laboratory staff you are taking this medicine.
For smoking cessation.
If you take bupropion to help you stop smoking, you may continue to smoke for about 1 week after you start the medicine.
Set a date to quit smoking during the second week of treatment.
Talk to your doctor if you are having trouble quitting after you have used bupropion for at least 7 to 12 weeks.
Your doctor may prescribe a nicotine replacement product (such as patches or gum) to help you stop smoking.
Start using the nicotine replacement product on the same day you stop (quit) smoking or using tobacco products.

You may have nicotine withdrawal symptoms when you stop smoking, including increased appetite, weight gain, trouble sleeping, trouble concentrating, slower heart rate, having the urge to smoke, and feeling anxious, restless, depressed, angry, frustrated, or irritated.
These symptoms may occur with or without using medication such as bupropion.
Smoking cessation may also cause new or worsening mental health problems, such as depression.

Cetirizine is used to treat cold or allergy symptoms such as sneezing, itching, watery eyes, or runny nose.

Pronunciation: sye kloe BEN za preen Brand names: Flexeril , Tonmya , Amrix , Fexmid Dosage form: immediate-release tablet (5 mg, 7.5 mg, 10 mg), extended-release capsule (15 mg, 30 mg), sublingual tablet (2.8 mg) Drug class: Skeletal muscle relaxants
Medically reviewed by Melisa Puckey, BPharm .
Last updated on Aug 14, 2026.
Cyclobenzaprine is a prescription muscle relaxant used short-term to relieve muscle spasms caused by sprains, strains, and injuries, including low back and neck pain.
It is used together with rest and physical therapy to help relieve the pain, tenderness, and limited movement caused by muscle spasm.
Cyclobenzaprine is also used to treat fibromyalgia in adults, where it can help reduce pain.
For fibromyalgia, it is taken as a sublingual (under the tongue) tablet at bedtime under the brand name Tonmya.
In clinical trials, Tonmya significantly reduced fibromyalgia pain compared with placebo over 14 weeks, and close to half of treated patients achieved at least a 30% improvement in pain.
The Flexeril brand has been discontinued, but cyclobenzaprine is available as generic tablets and as the brand-name products Amrix (extended-release capsules) and Fexmid.
Cyclobenzaprine works by reducing the nerve signals in the brain that drive muscle tone and spasm, which allows tight, overactive muscles to relax.
It acts within the central nervous system, primarily at the level of the brain stem, and does not act on the muscles themselves or at the junction between nerves and muscle.
1,2 Because cyclobenzaprine works through the nervous system in this way, it will not relieve muscle spasm caused by central nervous system disease, such as cerebral palsy or spinal cord disease.
The way cyclobenzaprine works in fibromyalgia is not known.
Laboratory studies show it blocks several receptor types, including serotonin (5-HT2A), histamine, and muscarinic receptors.

Cyclobenzaprine is chemically related to tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline, which explains several of its side effects (such as drowsiness and dry mouth) and some of its most important drug interactions.

Do not drive or do anything that needs alertness until you know how it affects you.

Overdose symptoms may include severe drowsiness, fast heartbeats, tremors, agitation, slurred speech, confusion, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, or hallucinations.
Rare but critical effects include seizures, dangerously low blood pressure, heart rhythm disturbances, and cardiac arrest.
Avoid driving or hazardous activity until you know how cyclobenzaprine will affect you.

The most common cyclobenzaprine side effects are drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, fatigue, and headache .
Most side effects are mild and settle as your body adjusts, but cyclobenzaprine can occasionally cause serious heart rhythm effects and serotonin syndrome.

With Amrix, the most common side effects are dry mouth (up to 14% at 30 mg), dizziness, fatigue, constipation, nausea, indigestion, and drowsiness.

With Tonmya, because it dissolves under the tongue, the most common side effects involve the mouth: reduced feeling or numbness in the mouth (23%), mouth discomfort, abnormal taste, tingling, mouth pain, and canker sores, along with sleepiness, fatigue, and dry mouth.
Mouth-related effects usually begin within minutes of a dose and most resolve within an hour.
Moistening your mouth with sips of water before dosing reduces the risk of numbness.
Tell your healthcare provider if mouth effects are severe.
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to cyclobenzaprine: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; or itching.
Stop taking cyclobenzaprine and call your doctor at once if you have: 1,2,3
fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeats;
chest pain or pressure, or pain spreading to your jaw or shoulder;
sudden numbness or weakness, slurred speech, or balance problems; or
symptoms of serotonin syndrome: agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness or twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Serious side effects, including confusion, hallucinations, and heart problems leading to falls, are more likely in older adults.
Yes, drowsiness is the most common side effect of the tablets, affecting up to 38% of people taking the 10 mg dose in clinical trials.
This is one reason 5 mg is the usual starting dose, since it causes less drowsiness with comparable effectiveness.
Analysis of trial data shows cyclobenzaprine relieves muscle spasm whether or not sedation occurs, so drowsiness is not required for it to work.
Constipation is a known side effect, reported in 1% to 3% of people taking the immediate-release tablets and up to 3% of people taking Amrix 30 mg in clinical trials.
It results from the drug's anticholinergic (drying) effects, the same mechanism behind dry mouth and blurred vision.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

The most serious cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril) drug interactions are with MAO inhibitors, which must never be combined with cyclobenzaprine, and with antidepressants and other serotonergic medicines, which can cause serotonin syndrome.
Cyclobenzaprine also interacts with alcohol and other medicines that cause drowsiness, making sedation worse.
Other medicines and substances that interact with cyclobenzaprine include: 1,2,3
MAO inhibitors such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, and tranylcypromine (contraindicated; do not use within 14 days);
antidepressants of any kind, including SSRIs, SNRIs, and tricyclics (risk of serotonin syndrome);
bupropion, tramadol, or meperidine;
verapamil;
alcohol;
opioid medicines, sleeping pills, other muscle relaxers, and medicines for anxiety or seizures;
barbiturates and other CNS depressants;
anticholinergic medicines;
guanethidine or similar blood pressure medicines;
cold or allergy medicines containing an antihistamine.
Cyclobenzaprine may increase the risk of seizures in people taking tramadol, and may block the blood pressure-lowering effect of guanethidine and similar drugs.
Tell your doctor about all your other medicines.
This list is not complete, and other drugs may interact with cyclobenzaprine, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.

sentence: Flexeril was the original brand name for cyclobenzaprine and remains the name many people know it by.

The Flexeril brand has been discontinued and is no longer on the marke t, but this was a commercial decision, not a safety withdrawal: generic cyclobenzaprine tablets containing the same active ingredient remain widely available and inexpensive.
Current brand names include Amrix (15 mg and 30 mg extended-release capsules taken once daily), Fexmid (7.5 mg tablets), and Tonmya (2.8 mg sublingual tablets for fibromyalgia, approved August 2025).
Is cyclobenzaprine a muscle relaxer?
Yes.
Cyclobenzaprine belongs to the class of medicines called skeletal muscle relaxants.
It relieves muscle spasm from acute painful muscle and skeletal conditions by acting in the central nervous system, not on the muscles directly.
What is cyclobenzaprine 10 mg used for?
The 10 mg tablet is used short-term (2 to 3 weeks) to relieve muscle spasm from acute painful conditions such as sprains and strains, alongside rest and physical therapy.
Treatment usually starts at 5 mg three times a day, increasing to 10 mg three times a day only if needed.
Is 10 mg of cyclobenzaprine strong?
10 mg is the highest recommended single dose of the tablet.
Clinical trials showed the 5 mg dose relieves muscle spasm about as well as 10 mg with less drowsiness, which is why 5 mg three times a day is the usual starting dose.
Does Tonmya work right away for fibromyalgia?

Tonmya starts at a lower dose for the first two weeks before increasing to the full dose, and in clinical trials pain relief was measured over 14 weeks of treatment, with benefits over placebo emerging progressively during that period.

The weight gain associated with Lexapro occurs primarily due to the drug's mechanism of action on serotonin levels in the brain.

When Lexapro blocks the serotonin transporter, it successfully increases serotonin availability to help treat depression and anxiety, but this same action can trigger unwanted changes in appetite and metabolism.
Lexapro (escitalopram) is usually taken once a day and can be taken either in the morning or at night.
Even though it takes Lexapro only a few hours to increase serotonin levels within the brain, it may take several weeks to start working.

Flonase is a nasal spray containing fluticasone propionate .
Fluticasone propionate is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation in the lining of the nose.
Flonase Nasal Spray is used to treat nasal congestion, sneezing, runny nose, and itchy or watery eyes caused by seasonal or year-round allergies .
Flonase Allergy Relief is for use in adults and children who are at least 4 years old and is available without a prescription.
Children's Flonase Allergy Relief contains the same medicine and is also for ages 4 and older.
Flonase Sensimist contains fluticasone furoate rather than fluticasone propionate and is approved for use in adults and children 2 years of age and older.
Children's Flonase Sensimist is also for ages 2 and older.
In Flonase Sensimist labeling, relief of itchy, watery eyes applies to ages 12 and older.
The brand-name prescription version of Flonase nasal spray has been discontinued in the United States.
Generic fluticasone propionate nasal spray is still available by prescription, and over-the-counter Flonase products and store brands remain on the market.
Some products sold under the Flonase brand name are not nasal sprays and do not contain fluticasone.
Flonase Headache & Allergy Relief caplets contain acetaminophen, chlorpheniramine, and phenylephrine, and Flonase Nighttime Allergy Relief tablets contain triprolidine.
Check the active ingredients on the carton before use.

Before using Flonase Nasal Spray, tell your doctor if you have glaucoma or cataracts, liver disease, diabetes, herpes simplex virus of your eyes, tuberculosis or any other infection, sores or ulcers inside your nose, or if you have recently had injury of or surgery on your nose.
You may start to feel relief on the first day, but it can take several days of regular once-daily use before you get the full effect.
Tell your doctor if your symptoms do not improve within 7 days, or if you develop new symptoms such as severe facial pain or thick nasal discharge.
Corticosteroids can affect the way your immune system responds to infection.
Avoid being near people who are sick or have infections.
Stop use and ask a doctor if you have, or come into contact with someone who has, chickenpox, measles, or tuberculosis.
Do not administer Flonase Allergy Relief Nasal Spray to a child younger than 4 years old, or Flonase Sensimist to a child younger than 2 years.
Corticosteroid medication can affect growth in children.
Talk with your doctor if you think your child is not growing at a normal rate while using this medicine.
Do not use Flonase nasal spray:
if you are allergic to fluticasone or to any of the other ingredients
to treat asthma
if you have had an injury to your nose, or surgery on your nose, that is not fully healed.
To make sure Flonase is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
sores or ulcers inside your nose;
injury of or surgery on your nose;
glaucoma or cataracts;
liver disease;
diabetes;
a weak immune system; or
any type of infection (bacterial, fungal, viral, or parasitic).
If you use Flonase without a prescription and you have any medical conditions, ask a doctor or pharmacist if this medicine is safe for you.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or breastfeeding.

Fluoxetine is a prescription antidepressant used to treat major depressive disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), bulimia nervosa, and panic disorder.
When used together with olanzapine (Zyprexa), it is also used to treat depressive episodes associated with bipolar I disorder and treatment-resistant depression.
Fluoxetine belongs to a class of antidepressants called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs).
The original brand name of fluoxetine is Prozac, and it's now available as a generic.
Fluoxetine is FDA-approved to treat the following conditions:
Major depressive disorder (MDD) for acute and maintenance treatment in adults and children aged 8 years and older
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) for acute and maintenance treatment in adults and children aged 7 years and older
Bulimia nervosa for acute and maintenance treatment of binge-eating and purging in adults with moderate to severe bulimia
Panic disorder for the treatment of panic attacks in adults
When used in combination with olanzapine, fluoxetine is also FDA-approved for:
Acute treatment of depressive episodes associated with Bipolar I disorder (depressive episodes) in adults and children aged 10 years and older
Treatment-resistant depression for adults who have not responded to at least two adequate antidepressant trials
Fluoxetine alone is not approved for bipolar I depressive episodes or treatment-resistant depression - olanzapine must be used in combination for these indications.
Fluoxetine works by blocking the reabsorption (reuptake) of serotonin in the brain, leaving more of it active between nerve cells.
Serotonin is a neurotransmitter that helps regulate mood, emotions, and sleep.
By increasing the availability of serotonin, fluoxetine can relieve symptoms of depression, anxiety, and OCD.
Fluoxetine belongs to a class of antidepressants called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) .
SSRIs are one of the most commonly prescribed antidepressant classes because they are generally well-tolerated and effective across a range of conditions.
Most people need to take fluoxetine for 4 to 6 weeks before feeling the full effects.
Like all medications, Prozac can cause side effects.
Not everyone experiences them, and many improve after the first few weeks as your body adjusts to the medication.
Tell your doctor if any side effects bother you or do not go away.

Nausea
Trouble sleeping (insomnia)
Drowsiness or sleepiness
Anxiety or feeling nervous or on edge
Trembling or shaking (tremor)
Excessive sweating

Diarrhea
Dry mouth
Indigestion or upset stomach
Weakness or fatigue
Sore throat
Sinus congestion or infection
Flu-like symptoms
Skin rash
Flushing or feeling of warmth
Yawning

Decreased sex drive

Like all medications, Prozac carries some important warnings you should be aware of before and during treatment.
Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following.
Fluoxetine carries a boxed warning, the FDA's most serious warning, regarding suicidal thoughts and behavior.

Antidepressants, including fluoxetine, may increase the risk of suicidal thoughts in children, adolescents, and young adult s , particularly in the first few months of treatment or when your dose is changed.
This risk was not seen in adults over 24, and adults 65 and older actually showed a reduced risk.
Anyone starting this medicine should be closely monitored for worsening mood or new or worsening suicidal thoughts, and families and caregivers should stay in regular contact with the prescriber.
Serotonin syndrome: A potentially life-threatening condition that can occur when serotonin builds up to dangerous levels.
This can occur when taken alone, but is more likely when taken with other serotonergic medications.
Seek emergency care immediately if you experience agitation, hallucinations, rapid heartbeat, high fever, muscle rigidity, tremor, or seizures.
Severe allergic reactions: Stop taking this medicine and seek emergency help if you develop trouble breathing, facial swelling, hives, or blistering rash.
Abnormal bleeding: This medicine may increase the risk of bleeding or bruising, particularly if taken with blood thinners (such as warfarin), NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen), or aspirin.
Eye problems (angle-closure glaucoma): This medicine can cause angle-closure glaucoma with symptoms of eye pain, vision changes, or swelling around the eye in some people.
An eye exam before starting treatment may be recommended for some people to assess their risk.
Seizures: Tell your doctor if you have a history of seizures before starting this medicine, or have conditions that potentially increase your risk of seizures

Changes in appetite or weight: Weight and appetite changes can occur, with some patients having significant weight loss.
Children and adolescents should have their height and weight monitored regularly during treatment.
Low sodium (hyponatremia): Low blood sodium levels can occur, particularly in older adults.
Symptoms include headache, weakness, confusion, and difficulty concentrating.
Heart rhythm changes (QT prolongation): Fluoxetine can affect the heart's electrical activity, potentially causing a serious and life-threatening irregular heartbeat.
Seek medical attention if you experience a fast, slow, or irregular heartbeat, shortness of breath, or fainting.
Sexual dysfunction: SSRIs, including fluoxetine, commonly affect sexual function.
In men, this may include delayed or absent ejaculation or erectile problems.
In women, it may include decreased libido or difficulty reaching orgasm.
Talk to your doctor if this occurs, as treatment options are available.
Drowsiness and impaired concentration: This medicine may affect your ability to think clearly, make decisions, or react quickly.

Anxiety and Insomnia: May occur in some patients while taking this medicine.
Blood sugar changes: People with diabetes may experience low blood sugar while taking this medicine, and high blood sugar when it is stopped.

Furosemide is a loop diuretic used to treat fluid retention (edema) in people with congestive heart failure, liver disease, or a chronic kidney disorder such as nephrotic syndrome.
Furosemide is also used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension).
Furosemide works by increasing the amount of urine the body makes, which helps reduce swelling and symptoms of fluid retention and helps lower high blood pressure.
Furosemide tablets are sometimes called water pills as they increase how much you urinate.
Furosemide is also known as frusemide in some countries.

It has been available in the United States since the 1960s and comes as tablets (Lasix), an oral liquid, an intravenous solution, and subcutaneous injections and infusions that can be given at home (Furoscix, Lasix ONYU).

Gabapentin is a prescription medicine used to treat partial seizures , nerve pain from shingles ( postherpetic neuralgia ), and restless legs syndrome (Horizant brand only).
It may also be prescribed off-label for other conditions including diabetic nerve pain, anxiety, and fibromyalgia.
Gabapentin is thought to work by calming overactive nerve signals in the brain and nervous system.
It is an anticonvulsant and nerve pain medication from the drug class gabapentinoids
Gabapentin brand names are Neurontin, Gralise, Horizant, and Relgaabi, which may not be interchangeable.

Gabapentin is not a federally controlled substance, but some states classify it as Schedule V and others require gabapentin prescriptions to be reported to their prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP).
Rules on refills and quantity limits vary by state.
The most common side effects of gabapentin are dizziness, drowsiness (somnolence), and swelling in the hands or feet (peripheral edema).
These often improve as your body adjusts, but do not drive until you know how gabapentin affects you.
Gabapentin is FDA-approved to treat partial onset seizures in patients 3 years and older (used with other seizure medicines) and nerve pain from shingles (postherpetic neuralgia) in adults.
A related product, gabapentin enacarbil (Horizant), is approved for moderate to severe restless legs syndrome in adults.
The approved uses depend on the specific product, and no single gabapentin product is approved for all of these conditions.
See the table below for a breakdown by brand.
Doctors also prescribe gabapentin off-label for other types of nerve pain, including diabetic nerve pain (diabetic neuropathy), and for anxiety, fibromyalgia, hot flashes, and alcohol withdrawal.
Off-label means that the condition it is being prescribed for is not an FDA-approved indication.
Different brands of gabapentin are not interchangeable, and they are FDA-approved for different conditions.
Use only the brand and form of gabapentin your doctor has prescribed.
Check your medicine each time you get a refill to make sure you receive the correct form.
Important: Gralise and Horizant are not substitutes for Neurontin or generic gabapentin, even at the same milligram dose.
The release profile differs, and switching without a prescriber's instruction can significantly change blood levels.
Sources: FDA prescribing information for Neurontin, Gralise, and Horizant; Relgaabi prescribing information (DailyMed)
Gabapentin works by calming overactive electrical signals in the brain and nervous system.

It does this by binding to the alpha-2-delta subunit of calcium channels in nerve cells, which is thought to normalize chemical signals nerves send to each other and results in a calmer, less excitable nerve circuit.
That same effect helps in different ways depending on what gabapentin is treating:
Epilepsy - dampens the runaway electrical firing that causes seizures.
Postherpetic neuralgia (shingles nerve pain) - reduces the abnormal pain signals from nerves damaged by shingles.
Restless legs syndrome (gabapentin enacarbil / Horizant) - the exact mechanism is less clear, but the same calming effect on overactive nerves is thought to ease the urge-to-move sensation.
Gabapentin is not an opioid, sedative, or anti-inflammatory painkiller.
It works directly on the nerves, which is why it helps nerve-related pain and why it isn't useful for everyday pain like headaches or sprains.
Most people need 1 to 2 weeks of regular dosing for the full effect to build up.

Gabapentin can cause life-threatening breathing problems (respiratory depression) , especially if you already have a breathing disorder (such as COPD), are elderly, or if you use other medicines that can make you drowsy or slow your breathing, such as opioids or CNS depressants.
Seek emergency medical attention if you have very slow breathing.

Some people have thoughts about suicide while taking and after discontinuing this medicine.
Stay alert to changes in your mood or symptoms.
Tell your doctor right away if you have any sudden changes in mood or behavior, or thoughts about suicide.
Abrupt or rapid discontinuation.
Seizures may occur if you stop using gabapentin suddenly.
Ask your doctor before stopping the medicine.
Stopping abruptly can cause withdrawal symptoms such as anxiety, trouble sleeping, nausea, pain, and sweating.
Sleepiness, sedation, and dizziness.

The most common side effects of gabapentin are dizziness, drowsiness (somnolence), swelling in the hands or feet (peripheral edema), and tiredness.

unsteadiness, poor coordination, or jerky movements
nausea or vomiting
headache
trouble speaking
blurred or double vision
tremor
signs of infection such as fever, chills, or sore throat
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to gabapentin: hives, difficult breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Seek medical treatment if you have a serious drug reaction that can affect many parts of your body.
Symptoms may include skin rash, fever, swollen glands, muscle aches, severe weakness, unusual bruising, or yellowing of your skin or eyes.

Tell your doctor right away if you have new or sudden changes in mood or behavior, including new or worse depression or anxiety, panic attacks, trouble sleeping, or if you feel impulsive, irritable, agitated, hostile, aggressive, restless, more active or talkative, or have thoughts about suicide or hurting yourself, while taking this medicine and after stopping it.
Gabapentin can slow or stop your breathing, especially if you have recently used an opioid medicine or alcohol.
A person caring for you should seek emergency medical attention if you have slow breathing with long pauses, blue-colored lips, or if you are hard to wake up.

You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Gabapentin can cause weight gain, although it is not common.
In clinical trials, a small number of people (roughly 2 in 100) gained weight while taking it.
Gabapentin can also cause swelling in the legs, feet, or hands (peripheral edema), which may add to weight changes and becomes more common with age.
You should not take gabapentin if you are allergic to it.

Pronunciation: HYE dro KLOR o THY a zide Generic name: Hydrochlorothiazide Brand names: HydroDIURIL (discontinued), Esidrix , Inzirqo , Microzide Dosage forms: oral capsule (12.5 mg), powder for oral suspension (10 mg/mL), oral tablet (12.5 mg; 25 mg; 50 mg) Drug class: Thiazide diuretics
Medically reviewed by Melisa Puckey, BPharm .
Last updated on Aug 28, 2026.
Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic , often called a water pill, used to treat high blood pressure and to reduce a build-up of fluid in the body ( edema ).
It works by making the kidneys pass more salt and water out of the body, so you urinate more.
Hydrochlorothiazide is often shortened to HCTZ on prescriptions and medical records.
It is available as a tablet, capsule, and liquid (suspension) taken by mouth and is usually taken once or twice a day.
Hydrochlorothiazide is available as:
oral tablet (12.5 mg, 25 mg, and 50 mg)
oral capsule (12.5 mg)
powder for oral suspension (10 mg/mL)
Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) brand names included HydroDIURIL tablets (discontinued), Esidrix (discontinued), and Microzide capsules (discontinued); now generic tablets and capsules are available.
The brand name of hydrochlorothiazide oral suspension is Inzirqo.
Hydrochlorothiazide is also an ingredient in many combination blood pressure medicines, including with losartan, lisinopril, valsartan, and more.
Hydrochlorothiazide is approved to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and fluid retention (edema) in certain patients.
HCTZ is used to manage high blood pressure (hypertension), either on its own or alongside other blood pressure medicines.
Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events, mainly strokes and heart attacks.
All three forms of hydrochlorothiazide, tablets, capsules and the oral suspension, are approved for high blood pressure in adults, and the oral suspension is also approved for children.
Hydrochlorothiazide tablets are used to treat a build-up of fluid (edema) associated with:
congestive heart failure
cirrhosis of the liver
kidney conditions, including nephrotic syndrome, acute glomerulonephritis and chronic kidney failure
treatment with corticosteroid or estrogen medicines

The HCTZ oral suspension is approved for fluid retention associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, and kidney disease including nephrotic syndrome, in both adults and children.
The capsules are approved for high blood pressure only, not for fluid retention.
Not all forms of HCTZ are approved for all indications and age groups.

Hydrochlorothiazide works by inhibiting the kidneys from reabsorbing sodium and chloride, so more salt and water leave the body in the urine, which helps reduce excess fluid buildup (edema).
Exactly how thiazides lower blood pressure is not fully understood.
The early effect is thought to come from a drop in blood volume.
With longer-term use, blood volume returns towards normal while the blood vessels themselves offer less resistance to blood flow.
Hydrochlorothiazide does not usually change blood pressure that is already normal.
Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic.
Do not take hydrochlorothiazide if you are unable to pass urine (anuria), or if you are allergic to hydrochlorothiazide or to other sulfonamide-derived medicines (sometimes called sulfa drugs).
Before you start HCTZ, tell your doctor if you have or have ever had:
kidney disease or reduced kidney function
liver disease, including cirrhosis
diabetes
gout or high uric acid levels
high cholesterol or high triglycerides
high calcium levels or a parathyroid gland disorder
low potassium or low sodium levels
lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus)
glaucoma
an allergy to sulfa medicines or to penicillin
Also tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.
Hydrochlorothiazide may cause jaundice or bleeding problems in a newborn.
It can also pass into breast milk and may cause serious side effects in a nursing baby, so you and your doctor should decide whether you will take this medicine or breastfeed.
Hydrochlorothiazide can lower the levels of potassium, sodium, magnesium and chloride in your blood.
Low potassium (hypokalemia) is the most common of these and is more likely at higher doses, during rapid fluid loss, if you have severe cirrhosis, or after long-term use..
Your doctor will check your blood before you start and at intervals during treatment.
Contact your doctor if you have any of the following, which can be signs of a fluid or salt imbalance:
dry mouth, thirst, or unusual weakness or tiredness
dry mouth, thirst, or unusual weakness or tiredness
drowsiness, restlessness or confusion
drowsiness, restlessness or confusion
muscle pain, cramps or muscle fatigue
muscle pain, cramps or muscle fatigue

passing much less urine than usual
nausea or vomiting
nausea or vomiting
seizures
seizures
HCTZ reduces the fluid volume in your body, which can lead to sudden kidney injury.
The risk is higher if you have chronic kidney disease, heart failure, or are already low on fluid.
If you have liver disease, small changes in fluid and salt balance can trigger a serious complication called hepatic coma.
Your doctor will monitor your kidney function and watch for changes in alertness.

section_title: What other drugs will affect hydrochlorothiazide?
sentence: Tell your doctor and pharmacist about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
Lithium.
Lithium and diuretics generally should not be taken together.
Hydrochlorothiazide reduces how quickly the kidneys clear lithium, which carries a high risk of lithium toxicity.
Cholestyramine and colestipol.
These cholesterol-lowering resins bind hydrochlorothiazide in the gut and can reduce how much you absorb by up to 85 percent for cholestyramine and 43 percent for colestipol.
The doses need to be separated.
For the oral suspension, the label advises taking hydrochlorothiazide at least 4 hours before, or 4 to 6 hours after, the resin.
NSAIDs such as ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), diclofenac, meloxicam, indomethacin, celecoxib and aspirin.
These can reduce the fluid-clearing and blood-pressure-lowering effects of hydrochlorothiazide, and your doctor will check whether the medicine is still working as intended.
Insulin and oral diabetes medicines.
Your diabetes medicine dose may need adjusting.
Corticosteroids and ACTH.
Taken with hydrochlorothiazide, these increase the loss of salts from the body, particularly potassium.
Digoxin and other digitalis medicines.
Low potassium caused by hydrochlorothiazide can make the heart more sensitive to the toxic effects of digitalis, including irregular heart rhythms.
Other blood pressure medicines.
The effects add together, which may be intended, but can also lower blood pressure more than expected.
Alcohol, barbiturates and opioid pain medicines.
These can make the drop in blood pressure on standing worse, causing dizziness or fainting.
Muscle relaxants used during surgery (nondepolarizing muscle relaxants such as tubocurarine).
You may respond more strongly to them, so tell your surgeon and anesthetist that you take hydrochlorothiazide.
Medicines that raise blood pressure (pressor amines such as norepinephrine).
Your response to them may be reduced, although this does not usually prevent their use.
This list is not complete.
Other medicines may affect hydrochlorothiazide, and hydrochlorothiazide may affect other medicines.
Hydrochlorothiazide is not a weight loss medicine.
Some people see the number on the scales drop in the first days or weeks of treatment, but this is extra fluid leaving the body rather than any loss of body fat, and it levels off.
Do not take hydrochlorothiazide to lose weight.

An overdose of acetaminophen and hydrocodone can be fatal.

Your caregiver must still get emergency medical help and may need to perform CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) on you while waiting for help to arrive.
Anyone can buy naloxone from a pharmacy or local health department.
Make sure any person caring for you knows where you keep naloxone and how to use it.
The first signs of an acetaminophen overdose include loss of appetite, nausea , vomiting , stomach pain, sweating, and confusion or weakness.
Later symptoms may include pain in your upper stomach, dark urine, and yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes.

Last updated on Sep 2, 2026.
Hydroxyzine is a prescription antihistamine used to treat anxiety and tension, itching from allergic skin conditions, and sedation before and after general anesthesia.
It comes in three oral forms:
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) tablets in 10 mg, 25 mg, and 50 mg strengths
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride oral solution (a syrup) containing 10 mg in each 5 mL
Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules in 25 mg
There is also a hydroxyzine hydrochloride injection.
It is given into a muscle by a healthcare professional and is never given into a vein or under the skin.
Hydroxyzine is not chemically related to benzodiazepines, phenothiazines, reserpine, or meprobamate.
Hydroxyzine taken by mouth is approved for three uses.
These are the same for hydroxyzine HCl and hydroxyzine pamoate.
Anxiety and tension.
For symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension linked to psychoneurosis, and as an add-on treatment in physical illnesses where anxiety is present.
Itching from allergic skin conditions.
For managing itching (pruritus) caused by allergic conditions such as long-term hives (chronic urticaria), eczema-type rashes, and rashes caused by contact with an irritant.
It is also used for itching caused by histamine release.
Sedation around surgery.
As a sedative given before a procedure (premedication) and after general anesthesia.
The injection is also approved for nausea and vomiting and is usually given in hospital or clinic settings.
It should not be used for nausea and vomiting caused by pregnancy.
Hydroxyzine has not been studied for long-term use in anxiety.
Studies have not assessed whether it still works as an anti-anxiety medicine beyond four months.
Your doctor should review from time to time whether you still need it.

Hydroxyzine is thought to work by quieting activity in certain deeper regions of the brain, below the outer layer known as the cortex.
It is not a cortical depressant, meaning it does not work by slowing down the outer layer of the brain the way some other sedatives do.
Hydroxyzine also blocks histamine, a chemical your body releases during an allergic reaction.
This is what relieves itching.
Laboratory and clinical studies have also shown that hydroxyzine relaxes skeletal muscle, widens the airways (bronchodilation), and reduces pain.
These are effects that have been observed rather than uses the medicine is approved for.
Hydroxyzine has also been shown to reduce nausea and vomiting.
This is an approved use for the injection, but not for the forms taken by mouth.
Take hydroxyzine exactly as your doctor prescribes.
Follow all directions on your prescription label.
Do not take more or less than prescribed, and do not take it for longer than your doctor tells you to.
Your doctor may adjust your dose depending on how well you respond to treatment.
If you are taking the oral solution, measure your dose with the dosing syringe provided, a dose-measuring spoon, or a medicine cup.
Do not use a kitchen spoon, because it will not give an accurate dose.
Ask your pharmacist for a measuring device if you do not have one.

sentence: If you develop a rash while taking hydroxyzine, stop taking it and call your doctor, because a rash can be the first sign of a serious reaction.
Common hydroxyzine side effects include dry mouth, headache, and drowsiness.
The drowsiness is usually temporary and may go away after a few days of treatment or when the dose is lowered.
Stop taking hydroxyzine and call your doctor right away if you develop a skin rash, if a skin condition you are treating gets worse, or if you have any other sign of an allergic reaction.
In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP).
Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin.
If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.
Other reported side effects include:
tremor or seizures (convulsions), which are rare and have usually happened at doses much higher than recommended
hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)
skin reactions including rash, hives, itching, and fixed drug eruptions, which are rashes that come back in the same spot each time the medicine is taken
allergic reaction
Serious breathing problems have not been reported at recommended doses.
If you are given hydroxyzine by injection, tell your healthcare provider straight away about severe pain, swelling, or skin changes where the injection was given.
In rare cases, the injection has caused serious damage to the surrounding tissue, including tissue death (necrosis) and gangrene, which has needed surgery to treat.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may happen.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Weight gain is not among the side effects reported in FDA-approved labeling for hydroxyzine.
It does not appear in the labeling for the tablets, the oral solution, the pamoate capsules, or the injection.
This does not mean weight changes are impossible for every person.
If your weight changes while you are taking hydroxyzine, tell your doctor.
Do not take hydroxyzine if you:
are allergic to hydroxyzine or to any ingredient in the medicine
are allergic to cetirizine or levocetirizine
have a prolonged QT interval, a heart rhythm finding seen on an electrocardiogram (ECG)
are in early pregnancy
In animal studies, hydroxyzine caused birth defects in rats and mice at doses well above those used in people.
There is not enough information in humans to know whether hydroxyzine is safe in early pregnancy, so it should not be used at that time.

Hydroxyzine is intended for short-term anxiety treatment only, typically less than 4 months.
Long-term hydroxyzine use is considered off-label because no studies have examined the safety of extended use beyond this timeframe.
Some research suggests a link between long-term use of medications with anticholinergic properties, such as hydroxyzine, and dementia, particularly in older adults.
Brain fog has also been reported with long-term use.

Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID).
It works by reducing hormones that cause inflammation and pain in the body.
Ibuprofen is used to reduce fever and treat pain or inflammation caused by many conditions such as headache , toothache , back pain , arthritis, menstrual cramps, or minor injury.
Ibuprofen is used in adults and children.
Some formulations are also used in premature babies to close a certain heart defect.
Ibuprofen can increase your risk of fatal heart attack , heart failure, or stroke.
Do not use this medicine just before or after heart bypass surgery (coronary artery bypass graft, or CABG).
Avoid taking ibuprofen after a recent heart attack, unless your doctor tells you to.
Ibuprofen may also cause stomach or intestinal bleeding, which can be fatal.
These conditions can occur without warning while you are using this medicine, especially in older adults.
Do not take more than your recommended dose.
An ibuprofen overdose can damage your stomach or intestines.
Use only the smallest amount of medication needed to get relief from your pain, swelling, or fever.
You should not use ibuprofen if you are allergic to it, or if you have ever had an asthma attack or severe allergic reaction after taking aspirin or an NSAID.

Insulin glargine is a long-acting insulin used to treat type 1 and type 2 diabetes in certain patients to improve and maintain blood glucose levels.
Insulin glargine is a man-made form of human insulin that is used once daily to provide a base level of insulin that keeps working for 24 hours or longer.
Insulin glargine is available under the brand names Lantus , Basaglar , Toujeo, Semglee , and Rezvoglar .
Langlara is an interchangeable biosimilar to Lantus that was FDA-approved on May 4, 2026.
Rezvoglar, Lantus, Langlara, Semglee, and Toujeo are FDA-approved to be used for use in adult and pediatric patients with type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
Basasglar is FDA-approved to be used by adults for type 2 diabetes and also for adults and pediatric patients with type 1 diabetes .
In patients with type 1 diabetes, insulin glargine must be used together with a short-acting insulin.

Common insulin glargine side effects may include low blood sugar , swelling, weight gain, allergic reaction, itching, rash, or thickening or hollowing of the skin where you injected the medicine (lipodystrophy).
Serious insulin glargine side effects

Get emergency medical help if you have signs of insulin allergy: redness or swelling where an injection was given, itchy skin rash over the entire body, trouble breathing, fast heartbeats, feeling like you might pass out, or swelling in your tongue or throat.
Insulin glargine may cause other serious side effects.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
rapid weight gain, swelling in your feet or ankles;
shortness of breath ; or
low blood potassium--leg cramps, constipation , irregular heartbeats, fluttering in your chest, increased thirst or urination, numbness or tingling, muscle weakness or limp feeling.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Never share an injection pen, even if you changed the needle.
You should not use insulin glargine if you are allergic to insulin, or if you are having an episode of hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) or diabetic ketoacidosis (call your doctor for treatment).
Different brands of insulin glargine are specifically approved for different age groups and different diabetes types.
The safety and effectiveness of insulin glargine in pediatric patients younger than 6 years of age with type 1 diabetes and pediatric patients with type 2 diabetes has not been established.
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
liver or kidney disease; or
heart failure or other heart problems.

Levothyroxine is a man-made form of thyroxine (T4), one of the hormones your thyroid gland normally produces.
It belongs to a class of medications called hormones, and it works by replacing thyroid hormone that your body is not making enough of.
Levothyroxine is used in adults and children, including newborn babies, to:
treat hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid - a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone).

It replaces the missing hormone whether the condition was present from birth or developed later, and whether the problem starts in the thyroid gland itself or in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus; and
lower the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the blood in people being treated for a certain type of thyroid cancer, alongside surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.
Levothyroxine injection is used in adults to treat myxedema coma, a rare and life-threatening complication of a severely underactive thyroid.
Without thyroid hormone, your body cannot function properly.

This may result in poor growth, slow speech, lack of energy, excessive tiredness, constipation, weight gain, hair loss, dry, thick skin, increased sensitivity to cold, joint and muscle pain, heavy or irregular menstrual periods, and depression.
When taken correctly, levothyroxine reverses these symptoms, although it may take several weeks before you notice a difference.
Levothyroxine is usually taken for life.

Levothyroxine may cause serious side effects.

sudden pain or trouble moving your hip, wrist, or back;
