changes in your menstrual periods, or difficulty getting pregnant; or
stomach cramps, vomiting, diarrhea.
Most of these side effects happen when the levothyroxine dose is higher than your body needs, which produces symptoms of an overactive thyroid.
Tell your doctor if you have any of them so your dose can be checked.

Children taking levothyroxine may also develop increased pressure around the brain (which can cause headaches, vomiting, or vision changes) or a hip problem called slipped capital femoral epiphysis, which causes hip, groin, or knee pain and limping.
Call your child's doctor about any of these symptoms.

Too much levothyroxine in babies can cause the soft spots on the skull to close too early, and in older children it can cause the growth plates to close too early, which may reduce final adult height.
Too little levothyroxine can affect a child's learning and growth.
This is why children need regular blood tests and check-ups.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Levothyroxine should not be used to treat obesity or weight problems.
Dangerous side effects or death can occur from the misuse of this medicine, especially if you are taking any other weight-loss medications or appetite suppressants.
Taking more than your recommended dose will not make this medicine more effective, and may cause serious side effects.
Levothyroxine has a narrow therapeutic index, which means the difference between too little and too much is small.
Taking too much or too little over time can affect your heart, bones, blood sugar, cholesterol, digestion, memory and concentration, fertility, and, in children, growth and development.
Your doctor will start you on a suitable dose and adjust it gradually based on blood tests.
You may not be able to use levothyroxine if you have certain medical conditions.
Tell your doctor if you have an untreated or uncontrolled adrenal gland disorder or any heart problems such as a recent heart attack.
If you have an adrenal gland problem, you will need to start treatment with a steroid (glucocorticoid) medicine before you start levothyroxine.
Starting levothyroxine first can trigger a sudden, serious drop in adrenal hormones known as an adrenal crisis.

Older adults and people with heart disease are usually started on a lower dose, because too much thyroid hormone can cause an irregular heartbeat (most commonly atrial fibrillation), angina, or other heart problems.
Tell your doctor if you develop chest pain, breathlessness, or a fast or irregular heartbeat.
Taking more levothyroxine than your body needs over a long period can weaken your bones and lead to a higher risk of fractures.
This is more likely after menopause.
Your doctor will aim to give you the lowest dose that controls your thyroid levels.
Oral levothyroxine should not be used to treat myxedema coma.
Levothyroxine given into a vein is used instead.
You should not use levothyroxine if you have an untreated or uncontrolled adrenal gland disorder.
You should not use certain liquid or injectable forms of levothyroxine if you are allergic to glycerin or edetate disodium.
To make sure this medicine is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
a thyroid nodule;
thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland);
heart problems such as a heart attack, stroke, angina, or an irregular heartbeat;
a blood clot or a blood clotting disorder;
diabetes (your diabetes medicine may need to be adjusted);
anemia (low red blood cells);
weak bones (osteoporosis), or low bone mineral density;
problems with your pituitary or adrenal gland;
an allergy to any food or drugs;
recently received radiation therapy with iodine (such as I-131); or
kidney disease.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.

Having hypothyroidism during pregnancy may increase the risk of miscarriage, high blood pressure in pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, stillbirth, or premature birth, and untreated hypothyroidism can affect the baby's brain development.
The benefit of treating hypothyroidism outweighs these risks, and levothyroxine should not be stopped during pregnancy.
Your dose needs are often higher during pregnancy.

Your doctor will check your thyroid blood tests as soon as your pregnancy is confirmed and at least once in each trimester, and will usually put you back on your pre-pregnancy dose straight after you give birth, with another blood test 4 to 8 weeks later.
Tell your doctor if you are breastfeeding.
Levothyroxine passes into breast milk, but no harmful effects on breastfed babies have been reported.
Treating hypothyroidism properly may also help milk supply if it is low.
Your dose needs may be different while you are nursing.
You may be more likely to have a broken bone while using levothyroxine, particularly if your dose is higher than you need.
Talk with your doctor about ways to keep your bones healthy.
Take levothyroxine exactly as prescribed by your doctor.
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.

Always check the instructions on the label.
Oral levothyroxine is taken by mouth and is available as tablets, capsules, and an oral solution.
Keep using this medicine even if you feel well.
It may take 4 to 6 weeks to get the full benefit of a dose.
You will need frequent medical tests, and your next dose may be delayed based on the results.
This medicine can affect the results of certain medical tests.
Tell any doctor who treats you that you are using this medicine.
Tell your doctor if you have a planned surgery or dental procedure.
Taking more than your recommended dose will not make this medicine more effective, and may cause serious side effects.
Take levothyroxine tablets and capsules on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast with a full glass of water.
A full glass of water is important to avoid choking or gagging, because the tablet can start to break apart quickly.
Take the medicine at the same time each day.
Swallow the capsule whole and do not crush, chew, break, or open it.
Tell your doctor if your child cannot swallow a capsule whole.
If you cannot swallow a tablet whole, crush the tablet and mix it with 1 or 2 teaspoons of water; give the mixture right away by spoon or dropper and make sure all of it is taken.
Do not save it for later use.
Do not mix it into soy-based infant formula or other foods that can stop levothyroxine being absorbed.
Keep each tablet or capsule in the blister pack until you are ready to take one.
Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).
Dosages are based on weight in children and teenagers.
Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of levothyroxine.
Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes.
Tirosint-Sol oral solution comes in single-dose ampules and can be administered 15 minutes before eating breakfast.
Squeeze the liquid directly into your mouth, onto a spoon, or into a glass of water to drink right away.
Use all ampules within 3 months after opening the foil pouch.
Ermeza and Thyquidity liquids should be taken on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast.
Store them in their original bottle.
Use Ermeza within 90 days and Thyquidity within 8 weeks of opening the bottle.
Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
This is given as an injection into a vein by a healthcare provider and should only be used to treat myxedema coma.
Your doctor will use blood tests to check that your dose is right, usually 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change, and then every 6 to 12 months once your dose is stable.
Children are tested more often, including 2 and 4 weeks after starting treatment and 2 weeks after any dose change.
Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you take biotin, or a multivitamin, hair, skin, or nail supplement that contains biotin (sometimes listed as vitamin B7).
Biotin can interfere with thyroid blood tests and give a falsely high or falsely low result, which could lead to the wrong dose change.
Stop biotin and any biotin-containing supplements at least 2 days before a thyroid blood test.

If your symptoms and blood tests still suggest an underactive thyroid even though you are on a dose that should be enough, it may be because the medicine is not being absorbed properly, doses are being missed, or another medicine is interfering.
Talk to your doctor before your dose is increased.

Generic name: lisinopril [ lyse-IN-oh-pril ] Brand names: Prinivil , Qbrelis , Zestril Dosage forms: oral solution (1 mg/mL), oral tablet (10 mg; 2.5 mg; 20 mg; 30 mg; 40 mg; 5 mg) Drug class: Angiotensin Converting Enzyme Inhibitors

Lisinopril is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children 6 years of age and older.
Lisinopril is also used in adults to treat congestive heart failure and to improve survival after a heart attack .
Lisinopril belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors.
It works by decreasing certain chemicals that tighten the blood vessels, so blood flows more smoothly and the heart can pump blood more efficiently.
High blood pressure is a common condition and when not treated, can cause damage to the brain, heart, blood vessels, kidneys, and other parts of the body.
Damage to these organs may cause heart disease, a heart attack, heart failure, stroke, kidney failure, loss of vision, and other problems.
In addition to taking medication, making lifestyle changes will also help to control your blood pressure.
These changes include eating a diet that is low in fat and salt, maintaining a healthy weight, exercising at least 30 minutes most days, not smoking, and using alcohol in moderation.
Do not use lisinopril if you are pregnant.
It could harm the unborn baby.

Usual Adult Dose for Hypertension:

Initial dose: 10 mg orally once a day; 5 mg orally once a day Maintenance dose: 20 to 40 mg orally once a day Maximum dose: 80 mg orally once a day Comments: -The initial dose is 5 mg orally once a day in patients receiving a diuretic.
-The 80 mg dose is used but does not appear to give greater effect.
-If blood pressure is not controlled with lisinopril alone, a low dose of a diuretic may be added (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, 12.5 mg).
After the addition of a diuretic, it may be possible to reduce the dose of lisinopril.
Usual Adult Dose for Congestive Heart Failure:

Initial dose: 2.5 to 5 mg orally once a day Maintenance dose: Dosage should be increased as tolerated Maximum dose: 40 mg orally once a day Comments: -The diuretic dose may need to be adjusted to help minimize hypovolemia, which may contribute to hypotension.
The appearance of hypotension after the initial dose of lisinopril does not preclude subsequent careful dose titration with the drug.
Usual Adult Dose for Myocardial Infarction:
Initial dose: 5 mg orally (within 24 hours of the onset of acute myocardial infarction) Subsequent doses: 5 mg orally after 24 hours, then 10 mg orally after 48 hours.
Maintenance dose: 10 mg orally once a day.
Dosing should continue for at least 6 weeks.
Comments: -Therapy should be initiated at 2.5 mg in patients with a low systolic blood pressure (less than or equal to 120 mm Hg and greater than 100 mmHg) during the first 3 days after the infarct.
If prolonged hypotension occurs (systolic blood pressure less than 90 mmHg for more than 1 hour) therapy should be withdrawn.
Uses: Reduction of mortality in acute myocardial infarction
Usual Adult Dose for Diabetic Nephropathy:
Initial dose: 10 to 20 mg orally once a day Maintenance dose: 20 to 40 mg orally once a day Dosage may be titrated upward every 3 days Comments: -Not an approved indication.
Usual Geriatric Dose for Hypertension:
Initial dose: 2.5 to 5 mg orally once a day Maintenance dose: Dosages should be increased at 2.5 mg to 5 mg per day at 1 to 2 week intervals.
Maximum dose: 40 mg orally once a day
Usual Pediatric Dose for Hypertension:

Pediatric patients greater than or equal to 6 years of age: Initial dose: 0.07 mg/kg orally once a day (Maximum initial dose is 5 mg once a day) Maintenance dose: Dosage should be adjusted according to blood pressure response at 1 to 2 week intervals.

Maximum dose: Doses above 0.61 mg/kg or greater than 40 mg have not been studied in pediatric patients Comments: -This drug is not recommended in pediatric patients less than 6 years old or in pediatric patients with glomerular filtration rate less than 30 mL/min.

Losartan is also used to decrease the risk of stroke in people who have high blood pressure and a heart condition called left ventricular hypertrophy (enlargement of the walls of the left side of the heart).

Losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin II receptor antagonists.

Metformin is a first-line treatment used for type 2 diabetes in adults and children 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar levels.
It is also used off-label to improve symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and other conditions.
Metformin tablets should be used together with dietary changes and exercise for better results.
Metformin belongs to the drug class biguanides .
Metformin works by reducing glucose absorption from the intestines, lowering liver glucose production, and improving insulin sensitivity.

Managing blood sugar levels with medications like metformin can prevent diabetes complications such as kidney damage, nerve issues, blindness, amputations, sexual dysfunction, and lower the risk of cardiovascular disease.
Metformin has a boxed warning for lactic acidosis , a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood, which can cause death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias.
A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA.

This is an extremely rare side effect but certain things can raise your risk of lactic acidosis, including kidney problems, taking certain other medicines, being over 65, having an imaging test that uses contrast dye, having surgery or other medical procedures, conditions that lower oxygen levels in the body, drinking too much alcohol, liver problems, and certain rare inherited metabolic disorders (mitochondrial diseases).
Stop taking metformin and call your healthcare professional immediately if you have any symptoms of lactic acidosis, including if you feel:
very weak and tired
have unusual (not normal) muscle pain
have trouble breathing
have unusual sleepiness or sleep longer than usual
have unexplained stomach or intestinal problems with nausea and vomiting, or diarrhea
cold, especially in your arms and legs
dizzy or lightheaded
have a slow or irregular heartbeat
Vitamin B12 deficiency: Metformin can lower your vitamin B12 levels over time.
Your doctor may check your blood counts every year and your B12 levels every 2 to 3 years to catch any problems early.

Low blood sugar when taken with insulin or other diabetes medicines: Taking metformin along with insulin or certain other diabetes drugs (ones that boost insulin release) raises the risk of low blood sugar.
If you're on one of these combinations, your doctor may lower the dose of the other medicine.

Macrovascular Outcomes: There have been no clinical studies that clearly show metformin reduces the risk of macrovascular disease, such as diseases or conditions that affect the coronary arteries, the aorta, and large arteries in the brain and limbs.
Common side effects of metformin hydrochloride tablets include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, wind (flatulence), indigestion, and headache.
These side effects occurred in 5% or more of patients in the US clinical trial of using metformin for type 2 diabetic patients.
In the same study, 6% of patients discontinued metformin due to diarrhea.

Less common side effects were abnormal stools, hypoglycemia, myalgia, lightheadedness, dyspnea, nail disorder, rash, increased sweating, taste disorder, chest discomfort, chills, flu syndrome, flushing, and palpitation, which occurred between 1% and less than 5% of patients.

Metformin is prescribed to manage polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) because it improves how the body responds to insulin.
PCOS affects about 1 in 10 women of reproductive age and is often marked by insulin resistance, in which the body doesn't respond well to insulin, prompting the pancreas to produce more.
This excess insulin drives up androgen (male hormone) production, worsening symptoms like irregular periods, infertility, acne, and excess hair growth.

Metformin helps by lowering insulin levels, decreasing the liver's glucose production, improving glucose uptake by muscles, and reducing circulating androgen levels as well, which can support more regular ovulation and menstrual cycles.

Although metformin is not FDA-approved to treat PCOS, it's widely prescribed as an off-label treatment, particularly for those with insulin resistance or fertility difficulties, and it's backed by extensive research and clinical guidelines.

Beyond helping regulate cycles and support ovulation, metformin may also help reduce androgen-related symptoms such as acne and excess hair growth, and can aid with weight management for those affected by PCOS-related weight gain.

Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack.
It works mainly on the heart, so it is called a cardioselective beta-blocker.
Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart.
This slows your heart rate, reduces how hard your heart squeezes, and lowers your blood pressure.
Because the heart is doing less work, it needs less oxygen, which is why metoprolol also helps with angina.
Exactly how metoprolol works for high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack is not fully understood.
At higher blood levels, metoprolol also blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways and blood vessels, which is why it still needs care in people with breathing problems.
Metoprolol comes as two different salts, metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate.
They are not interchangeable dose for dose:
Metoprolol tartrate , an immediate-release tablet usually taken once or twice a day (brand name Lopressor)
Metoprolol succinate , an extended-release tablet or capsule taken once a day (brand names Toprol-XL and Kapspargo Sprinkle)
Metoprolol tartrate is also given as an injection into a vein in a hospital during a heart attack.
Metoprolol is FDA-approved to treat high blood pressure, angina, heart failure, and heart attack, but the two forms are not approved for the same conditions.

Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of fatal and non-fatal heart and blood vessel events, mainly strokes and heart attacks.

The most common side effects of metoprolol are tiredness, dizziness, low mood (depression), diarrhea, shortness of breath, a slow heartbeat (bradycardia), and itching or rash.
Most side effects reported in studies were mild and did not last.
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to metoprolol: hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
In studies of people taking metoprolol for high blood pressure or angina:
Tiredness and dizziness occurred in about 10% of people
Low mood or depression was reported in about 5 out of 100 people
Diarrhea occurred in about 5% of people
Itching or rash occurred in about 5% of people
Shortness of breath and a slow heartbeat occurred in about 3% of people
Cold hands and feet, palpitations, swelling of the ankles, and low blood pressure were each reported in about 1% of people
Nausea, dry mouth, stomach pain, constipation, gas, and heartburn were each reported in about 1% of people
Headache, nightmares, trouble sleeping, confusion, and short-term memory loss have also been reported.

In the heart failure study of extended-release metoprolol, dizziness or vertigo was reported by 1.8% of people taking metoprolol compared with 1.0% taking placebo, and a slow heartbeat by 1.5% compared with 0.4%.
These have been reported since metoprolol came on the market.
Their frequency is not known:
Hair thinning or hair loss, which reversed after stopping
Reduced sex drive and difficulty getting an erection
Dry eyes, blurred vision, and ringing in the ears
Sweating, sensitivity to sunlight, and worsening of psoriasis
Change in taste, joint and muscle pain, and fainting
Liver inflammation (hepatitis)
A severe drop in white blood cells (agranulocytosis), which can show up as fever, chills, or a sore throat
Some of these, such as shortness of breath and a slow heartbeat, are also listed as common side effects above.
They need urgent attention when they are severe, new, or getting worse.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
A very slow heartbeat, pauses in your heartbeat, or a feeling that you might faint.
Sinus pause, heart block, and cardiac arrest have all been reported.
Signs that heart failure is getting worse, such as weight gain over a few days, more shortness of breath, or swelling of your feet or lower legs
Wheezing or trouble breathing
Chest pain that is worse or more frequent than usual, especially if you have recently stopped or missed doses
Cold, pale, or blue fingers and toes, or pain in your legs when you walk
Confusion, hallucinations, or memory problems
Yellowing of your skin or eyes, which can be a sign of liver inflammation
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
The most important warning with metoprolol is not to stop it suddenly.
Stopping a beta blocker abruptly can bring on worse chest pain and, in some cases, a heart attack.
If your treatment needs to stop, your prescriber will lower the dose gradually over 1 to 2 weeks and watch how you respond.
This applies even if you only take metoprolol for blood pressure, because heart disease is common and is not always known about.
Talk to your care team before starting metoprolol if any of these apply to you.
Asthma or other breathing problems.
Beta blockers can tighten the airways.
Metoprolol is used in people with these conditions only when other treatments are not suitable, at the lowest possible dose, with a reliever inhaler on hand.
Heart failure.
Heart failure can get worse while the dose is being increased.
Tell your doctor about weight gain or increasing breathlessness.
A slow heart rate or a conduction problem in the heart.
This includes first-degree heart block, sinus node problems, and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
Your heart rate should be monitored.
Diabetes or long gaps without food.
Metoprolol can hide the early warning signs of low blood sugar, such as a fast heartbeat, and can make low blood sugar more severe or last longer.
The risk is higher if you are fasting, not eating regularly, or vomiting.

Metoprolol can mask signs of an overactive thyroid.
Stopping it suddenly can trigger a thyroid crisis.
Circulation problems in your arms or legs.
Beta blockers can make symptoms of poor circulation worse.
A history of severe allergic reactions.
If you have anaphylaxis while taking a beta blocker, the usual dose of injectable epinephrine may not work as well.

Metoprolol must only be started after an alpha blocker has been started, or blood pressure can rise sharply.

Metoprolol is broken down by the liver, so levels can build up.
Treatment is usually started at a lower dose.

Tell your surgeon and dentist that you take metoprolol.
Long-term beta blocker treatment is not usually stopped before surgery.

Starting a high dose of extended-release metoprolol shortly before non-cardiac surgery is avoided, because in one large trial this was linked to more slow heartbeats, low blood pressure, strokes, and deaths.

You are then switched to metoprolol tablets.

Usual Adult Dose for Erosive Esophagitis:
Treatment of Erosive Esophagitis: 40 mg orally once a day for up to 8 weeks; however an additional 8 weeks may be considered for patients who have not healed after the initial treatment.

Maintenance of Healing of Erosive Esophagitis: 40 mg orally once a day.

Usual Adult Dose for Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease:
Parenteral: 40 mg once a day for 7 to 10 days, administered via intravenous infusion over a period of 15 minutes.
Intravenous therapy should be discontinued as soon as the patient is able to resume oral therapy.
Oral: 40 mg orally once a day, for short-term administration (up to 8 weeks); however an additional 8 weeks may be considered for patients who have not healed after the initial treatment.

Usual Adult Dose for Duodenal Ulcer:
Study (n=54) 40 mg orally once a day, dose was increased every 12 weeks by 40 mg increments to a maximum of 120 mg per day, for 28 weeks.
Data have revealed that monotherapy with daily doses of 40 mg have been associated with complete duodenal ulcer healing in up to 87% and 94% of patients after 4 weeks and 8 weeks respectively.

40 mg orally once a day.
Data have revealed that monotherapy with daily doses of 40 mg have been associated with complete gastric ulcer healing in up to 87% and 97% of patients after 4 weeks and 8 weeks respectively.

Study (n=242) - Triple therapy: 40 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, commonly in conjunction with clarithromycin and either amoxicillin or metronidazole to eradicate Helicobacter pylori, followed with 40 mg pantoprazole orally once daily until day 28.
Triple therapy has resulted in eradication rates of greater than 95%.

Helicobacter Pylori eradication was achieved in 82% of patients.

Parenteral: 80 mg every 12 hours, administered by 15-minute infusion.

Pronunciation: PRED-ni-sone Brand names: Rayos , Prednisone Intensol, Sterapred (discontinued), Deltasone (discontinued) Dosage form: tablets (1 mg, 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, and 50 mg), oral solution (5 mg/5 mL, 5 mg/mL) Drug class: Glucocorticoids
Medically reviewed by Melisa Puckey, BPharm .
Last updated on Sep 3, 2026.
Prednisone is a prescription corticosteroid (steroid) used to reduce inflammation, suppress an overactive immune system, and treat endocrine and metabolic disorders.

Prednisone is used for a wide range of conditions, including severe allergies , asthma and COPD flare-ups , rheumatoid arthritis and other forms of arthritis , lupus , psoriasis and other skin conditions, ulcerative colitis , Crohn's disease , eye inflammation, some blood disorders, and low adrenal hormone levels.
Prednisone works by mimicking the effects of glucocorticoid hormones secreted naturally by our adrenal glands.
Prednisone is a man-made (synthetic) version of these hormones.
Prednisone is different from steroids taken to build muscle (anabolic steroids).
Prednisone belongs to the drug class called glucocorticoids, which are a type of corticosteroid.
Prednisone tablets come in 1 mg, 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, and 50 mg strengths.
Prednisone 20 mg and prednisone 10 mg tablets are the strengths most often used for short courses in adults .
Prednisone also comes as a delayed-release tablet (Rayos), as an oral liquid, and as a concentrated oral solution (Prednisone Intensol) that is measured with a special dropper.
Many of the original brands are discontinued; however, generic prednisone is available.

The most common prednisone side effects are trouble sleeping, mood changes, increased appetite and weight gain, fluid retention and swelling, increased sweating, acne, thinning skin that bruises easily, slow wound healing, higher blood sugar, indigestion and stomach upset.
Many of these effects are dose related.
They are more likely on higher doses and on longer courses, and most settle after the medicine is stopped.
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to prednisone: hives, difficult breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
signs of infection, such as fever, chills, sore throat, cough or a wound that is not healing, since prednisone can hide the usual warning signs;
blurred vision, eye pain or seeing halos around lights, which can be signs of glaucoma (raised pressure in the eye) or cataracts;
severe pain in your upper stomach that spreads to your back, with nausea and vomiting, which can be a sign of pancreatitis (inflamed pancreas);
bloody or black, tarry stools, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds, which can be signs of a bleeding stomach ulcer;
severe depression, unusual excitement, confusion, changes in personality or behavior, or a seizure;
swelling, rapid weight gain or shortness of breath, which can be signs of fluid retention or heart failure;
signs of low potassium, such as confusion, an uneven heartbeat, extreme thirst, passing more urine than usual, leg discomfort, or muscle weakness;
a very high blood pressure reading with severe headache, blurred vision, ringing in your ears, chest pain or shortness of breath;
sudden pain, swelling or bruising in a tendon, especially at the back of the ankle, since prednisone can weaken tendons and cause the Achilles tendon to rupture;
new bone pain, especially in a hip, shoulder or knee, which can be a sign of aseptic necrosis (bone tissue that has lost its blood supply); or
flat, painless spots that are red or purple on light skin, or bluish, brown or black on dark skin, which can be a sign of Kaposi's sarcoma.
Women taking prednisone may notice irregular or missed periods, unwanted facial hair growth, acne and changes in body fat, such as a rounder face and more fat around the neck and waist.
Long courses of prednisone also raise the risk of osteoporosis (thinning of the bones), and postmenopausal women are already at higher risk.
Ask your doctor whether you need a bone density scan or a calcium and vitamin D supplement.

Taking prednisone for months or years raises the risk of osteoporosis and broken bones, muscle weakness and muscle loss, cataracts and glaucoma, diabetes, high blood pressure, Cushing's syndrome (a set of changes caused by too much steroid, including a rounded face and fat around the trunk), and adrenal suppression, where your body stops making enough of its own steroid hormones.
Children who take prednisone for a long time may grow more slowly.
Your child's doctor should check their growth at regular visits.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Do not take prednisone if you have a systemic fungal infection, which is a fungal infection that has spread through your body.
Prednisone weakens your immune system.
This makes it easier to get an infection; an existing infection may become worse and can reactivate an old infection, such as tuberculosis or hepatitis B.
It can also hide the usual signs of infection, so an infection may be advanced before you notice it.
Tell your doctor about any illness or infection you have had in the past few weeks.
Stay away from people who are sick.
Chickenpox and measles can be serious or even fatal in someone taking a steroid.
Call your doctor straight away if you are exposed to either one.
Do not have a live vaccine while you are taking prednisone unless your doctor says it is safe.
Do not stop taking prednisone suddenly after more than a few days of treatment.
Your body needs time to start making its own steroid hormones again.
Your doctor will lower your dose in steps.

Call your doctor at once if you have shortness of breath, severe pain in your upper stomach, bloody or black stools, severe depression, changes in personality or behavior, vision problems, or eye pain.
You should not use prednisone if you are allergic to it, or if you have a systemic fungal infection.
To make sure prednisone is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have or have ever had:
an infection of any kind, including tuberculosis, hepatitis B, herpes infection of the eye, or a fungal infection;
diarrhea that has no clear cause, or time spent in the tropics, since prednisone can wake up a parasite infection such as amebiasis or threadworm;
malaria, especially cerebral malaria (malaria affecting the brain);
liver disease, such as cirrhosis;
kidney disease;
heart disease, heart failure, high blood pressure or low potassium levels;
an underactive thyroid;
diabetes;
osteoporosis;
glaucoma or cataracts;
stomach ulcers, ulcerative colitis, diverticulitis, or a history of bleeding in the stomach or bowel;
myasthenia gravis (a condition that causes muscle weakness); or
depression, mood swings or another mental health condition.
Long-term steroid use can cause bone loss.
Your risk is higher if you smoke, if you do not exercise, if you do not get enough calcium or vitamin D, or if osteoporosis runs in your family.
Talk with your doctor about protecting your bones.
Prednisone crosses the placenta.
Taking it in the first trimester may raise the risk of birth defects, and taking higher doses later in pregnancy may affect the baby's growth and their adrenal glands.
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
Some conditions still need steroid treatment during pregnancy, so this is a decision to make with your doctor rather than stopping on your own.
Prednisone passes into breast milk in small amounts.
Tell your doctor if you are breastfeeding so you can talk through the dose and the timing of feeds.
Prednisone is used in children, but long courses can slow growth and affect bone development.
The dose should not be higher than prescribed, and your child should be monitored during treatment.
Older adults are more likely to have liver, kidney, or heart problems that affect how prednisone is handled, and are more likely to already have osteoporosis, diabetes, or high blood pressure.
A lower dose may be needed.
Take prednisone exactly as prescribed, with food or milk to protect your stomach.
Your doctor will often start you on a higher dose and then lower it.
Do not change your dose or stop the medicine without advice.
Take your dose in the morning if your doctor tells you to.
Your adrenal glands are most active between 2 am and 8 am, and taking a steroid at that time interferes with them the least.
A morning dose may also help you sleep better, though that is a separate benefit.
Swallow delayed-release tablets whole.
Do not crush, break, or chew them.
Measure liquid prednisone with a marked oral syringe, dosing spoon or medicine cup, not a kitchen spoon.
Use the dropper that comes with the concentrated solution.
You may mix the concentrated solution with juice or a soft food such as applesauce.
Tell your doctor if you have a serious illness, a fever, an infection, surgery, or a medical emergency.
You may need a higher dose for a short time.
You may need regular blood tests, blood pressure checks and eye checks during long-term treatment.
Wear a medical alert tag or carry a card saying you take a steroid.
Store prednisone at room temperature, away from moisture and heat.
Throw away any unused concentrated solution 90 days after you first open the bottle.

Rosuvastatin (Crestor) is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events such as heart attack and stroke.
Rosuvastatin belongs to a class of medicines called statins.
It works by blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol.
With cholesterol synthesis reduced, the liver increases its LDL receptors and clears more LDL, or "bad" cholesterol, from the blood.
LDL and total cholesterol levels fall, with the maximum reduction usually reached by four weeks.
Rosuvastatin comes as a tablet.
It was first approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on August 12, 2003, under the brand name Crestor.
Many generic versions of rosuvastatin tablets have since been approved.
Rosuvastatin is used:

to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular (CV) events, such as death from cardiovascular disease, heart attack, stroke, or the need for procedures to improve blood flow to the heart called arterial revascularization, in adults at increased risk for these events.
along with diet and exercise to lower the level of low-density lipoprotein (LDL-C) cholesterol or "bad" cholesterol: in adults with primary hypercholesterolemia.
and slow the buildup of fatty deposits (plaque) in the walls of blood vessels in adults.
in adults and children 8 years of age and older with high blood cholesterol due to heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) (an inherited condition that causes high levels of LDL-C).
in adults and children 7 years of age and older with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HoFH) (an inherited condition that causes high levels of LDL-C).

It is not known if rosuvastatin is safe and effective in children younger than 8 years of age with HeFH, children younger than 7 years of age with HoFH, or in children with other types of hypercholesterolemia (other than HeFH or HoFH).
The most common side effects may include headache, nausea, muscle aches and pains, weakness, and constipation.

Semaglutide ( Ozempic , Wegovy , Rybelsus ) is a prescription GLP-1 medication used for weight loss and weight management, type 2 diabetes treatment, or to reduce the risk of chronic kidney disease and major cardiovascular events in certain patients with type 2 diabetes.
Semaglutide (Wegovy) is also used to treat metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), without cirrhosis of the liver.
Semaglutide injections are self-administered once weekly as an injection under the skin, and semaglutide pills are taken once daily.
Semaglutide works by reducing appetite, delaying gastric emptying, increasing insulin release, and lowering the amount of glucagon released.
Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist that mimics the behavior of the GLP-1 hormone, which is naturally released after eating.
Semaglutide brand names are Ozempic, Rybelsus, and Wegovy, all made by Novo Nordisk.
There is no generic semaglutide available.
Semaglutide FDA approval was first granted on December 5, 2017, for the brand Ozempic.
Each semaglutide brand or formulation is FDA-approved for specific conditions and patient populations.

Semaglutide FDA-approved uses for each brand are Ozempic (type 2 diabetes, reducing cardiovascular event risks, reducing risk of kidney function decline), Wegovy (weight management, reducing cardiovascular event risks, non-cirrhotic MASH), and Rybelsus (type 2 diabetes, reducing cardiovascular event risks).
Semaglutide should be used in addition to a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.
Ozempic tablets and injections are FDA-approved in adults for:
type 2 diabetes to improve blood sugar control
reducing the risk of a major cardiovascular event (such as heart attack, stroke, or death) in type 2 diabetic patients who are at high risk for these events
Ozempic injection is also FDA-approved in adults for:
reducing the risk of kidney function decline , kidney failure, and cardiovascular death in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (CKD)
Wegovy tablets and injections are FDA-approved in adults for:
weight loss and weight management in adults with obesity or adults who are overweight and have a weight-related medical problem (e.g., blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, or high cholesterol)
reducing major cardiovascular event risks (such as heart attack, stroke, or death) in adults with established CV disease and either obesity or overweight
Wegovy injection is also FDA-approved for:
weight loss and weight management patients with obesity who are 12 years and older
non-cirrhotic metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) in adults with moderate to advanced liver fibrosis (consistent with stages F2 to F3 fibrosis), this is an accelerated approval.
Rybelsus oral tablets are FDA-approved in adults for:
type 2 diabetes in adults to help control blood sugar levels.
reducing the risk of major cardiovascular events (such as heart attack, stroke, or death) in type 2 diabetic patients with known heart disease.
Also, see Wegovy vs Ozempic: Which is right for you?

Semaglutide works by:
Stimulates insulin production in the pancreas
Reduces sugar production in the liver
Slows down digestion, so food stays in the stomach longer
Decreases appetite and food intake
These combined actions help you feel full longer, eat less, and maintain better control over blood sugar levels.
As a result, semaglutide supports weight loss , improves blood sugar management , and helps reduce the risk of cardiovascular events .
Semaglutide's mechanism of action mimics a natural hormone in the body called GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1), which is released after eating to help regulate appetite and blood sugar levels.
The way semaglutide works for kidney-related risk reduction is not fully understood.
Semaglutide belongs to the drug class called GLP-1 receptor agonists.

Common semaglutide side effects may include upset stomach , heartburn , burping , gas, bloating, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, loss of appetite, diarrhea, constipation, stomach flu symptoms, low blood sugar (in people with type 2 diabetes), headache, dizziness, tiredness, hair loss, and changes in skin sensations.
Stomach or gastrointestinal side effects are common, but they tend to be mild and clear up in a few weeks and usually will not interfere with long-term treatment.
Stomach side effects can be more common with higher doses.
Following these tips may help you manage stomach semaglutide side effects:
Eat more slowly
Eat smaller meals
Choose more bland, low-fat foods (like crackers, toast, and rice)
Avoid eating greasy, fried foods or sugar treats
Eat foods that contain water (like soup or gelatin)
Do not lie down right after eating
Drink clear or ice-cold liquids
If possible, go outside for fresh air if you feel sick to your stomach
Ryebelsus is not recommended in patients with severe gastroparesis.

Test blood sugar levels regularly if you are also taking diabetic medicines, including insulin or sulphonylureas (e.g., glibenclamide/glyburide, glipizide, and gliclazide) and when you increase your semaglutide dose.
Your prescriber might reduce your dose of insulin or sulphonylureas if needed to reduce the risk of hypoglycemia
Symptoms of low blood sugar levels include:
feeling hungry
feeling dizzy
feeling anxious or irritable
sweaty
shaky
tingling lips
heart palpitations
feeling tired or weak
changes in your vision, such as blurred vision
confusion
Treatment for hypoglycemia

Eat or drink something that will raise your blood sugar quickly for example, sugary foods or drinks, including a small glass of fruit juice or sugary fizzy drink (not diet), glucose or dextrose tablets or gel, or sugary candy.
Check your blood sugar after 10 to 15 minutes.
If your blood sugar is still low, have another sugary drink or snack, and check again after 10 minutes.
Once your symptoms have improved, eat a healthy snack or meal that will keep your blood sugar up for longer and prevent another drop in blood sugar.
Severe hypoglycemia may require a glucagon injection.
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction: hives , itching, dizziness, fast heartbeats, difficulty breathing, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
vision changes;
unusual mood changes, thoughts about hurting yourself;
pounding heartbeats or fluttering in your chest;
a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out;
signs of a thyroid tumor - swelling or a lump in your neck, trouble swallowing, a hoarse voice, feeling short of breath;
symptoms of pancreatitis - severe pain in your upper stomach spreading to your back, nausea with or without vomiting, fast heart rate ;
gallbladder problems - upper stomach pain, fever, clay-colored stools, jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes);
low blood sugar - headache , hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery;
kidney problems - swelling, urinating less, feeling tired or short of breath; or
stomach flu symptoms - stomach cramps, vomiting, loss of appetite, diarrhea (may be watery or bloody); or severe stomach problems like severe constipation, fecal impaction, or intestinal obstruction.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Semaglutide has a boxed warning for the risk of thyroid C-cell tumors.
A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA.
Semaglutide may cause serious side effects, including possible thyroid tumors and thyroid cancer .
Call your doctor at once if you have signs of a thyroid tumor, such as swelling or a lump in your neck, trouble swallowing, a hoarse voice, or shortness of breath.
You should not use semaglutide if you have multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (tumors in your glands) or a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer .

Semaglutide also has warnings for pancreatitis, diabetic retinopathy complications, hypoglycemia that can be severe, acute kidney injury, acute gallbladder disease, hypersensitivity reactions, and pulmonary aspiration during general anesthesia or deep sedation.
For Wegovy, there are also warnings for a heart rate increase and suicidal behaviour or ideation.
For Rybelsus, there is also a warning for severe gastrointestinal side effects.
You should not use semaglutide if you are allergic to it, or if you have:
multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (tumors in your glands);
a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (a type of thyroid cancer); or
diabetic ketoacidosis (call your doctor for treatment).
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
a stomach or intestinal disorder;
pancreatitis ;
are planning surgery or other procedure that uses anesthesia or deep sedation;
kidney disease; or
eye problems caused by diabetes ( retinopathy ).
In animal studies, semaglutide caused thyroid tumors or thyroid cancer.
It is not known whether these effects would occur in people.
Ask your doctor about your risk.
Men and women should stop using semaglutide at least 2 months before they plan to get pregnant.
Ask your doctor for a safer medicine to use during this time.
Controlling diabetes is very important during pregnancy, as is gaining the right amount of weight.
Even if you are overweight, losing weight during pregnancy could harm the unborn baby.
There is a pregnancy exposure registry for women who use Wegovy during pregnancy.
The purpose of this registry is to collect information about the health of you and your baby.
Talk to your healthcare provider about how you can take part in this registry or contact Novo Nordisk at 1-877-390-2760 or www.wegovypregnancyregistry.com.
Ask a doctor if it is safe to breastfeed while using Ozempic or Wegovy injections.
Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment with Wegovy tablets.
You should not breastfeed while using Rybelsus.
Semaglutide injections ( Ozempic and Wegovy) are injected under the skin, usually once per week at any time of the day, with or without food.
Use an injection on the same day each week.
Read and follow all instructions you have been given.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you need help.
Prepare an injection only when you are ready to give it.
Call your pharmacist if the medicine looks cloudy, has changed colors, or has particles in it.
Your healthcare provider will show you where to inject semaglutide.
Do not inject into the same place twice in a row.
If you are visually impaired, the Wegovy FlexTouch pen is not recommended for self-injection.
If you choose a different weekly injection day, start your new schedule after at least 2 days have passed since the last injection you gave.
Do not use different brands of semaglutide at the same time.

Semaglutide oral tablets (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus) are taken once a day at least 30 minutes before the first food, beverage, or other oral medications of the day with no more than 4 ounces of plain water only.
After 30 minutes of taking the tablet, you may eat, drink, or take other oral medicines.
Swallow tablets whole.
Do not split, crush, or chew tablets.
Blood sugar can be affected by stress , illness, surgery, exercise, alcohol use, or skipping meals.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can make you feel very hungry, dizzy, irritable, or shaky.
To quickly treat hypoglycemia , eat or drink hard candy, crackers, raisins, fruit juice, or non-diet soda.
Your doctor may prescribe glucagon injections in case of severe hypoglycemia.
Tell your doctor if you have frequent symptoms of high blood sugar (hyperglycemia), such as increased thirst or urination.
Ask your doctor before changing your dose or medication schedule.
Your treatment may also include diet, exercise, weight control, medical tests, and special medical care.
You may get dehydrated during prolonged illness.
Call your doctor if you are sick with vomiting or diarrhea , or if you eat or drink less than usual.
Never share an injection pen, even if you changed the needle.
Sharing an injection can pass infection or disease from person to person.
The Ozempic injection pen contains more than one dose.
After your first use, store the pen with the needle removed in a refrigerator or at room temperature.
Protect from heat and light.
Keep the cap on when not in use.
Throw the pen away 56 days after the first use or if less than 0.25 mg is shown on the dose counter.
Do not reuse a needle.
Place it in a puncture-proof "sharps" container and dispose of it following state or local laws.
Keep out of the reach of children and pets.
Start Ozempic with a 0.25 mg subcutaneous injection (injection under the skin) once weekly for 4 weeks.
The 0.25 mg dosage is intended for treatment initiation and is not effective for glycemic control.
After 4 weeks on the 0.25 mg dosage, increase the dosage to 0.5 mg once weekly.
If additional glycemic control is needed after at least 4 weeks on the 0.5 mg dosage, the dosage may be increased to 1 mg once weekly.
If additional glycemic control is needed after at least 4 weeks on the 1 mg dosage, the dosage may be increased to 2 mg once weekly.
The maximum recommended dosage is 2 mg once weekly.
Administer Ozempic once weekly, on the same day each week, at any time of the day, with or without meals.
The day of weekly administration can be changed if necessary, as long as the time between two doses is at least 2 days (>48 hours).
If a dose is missed, administer Ozempic as soon as possible within 5 days after the missed dose.
If more than 5 days have passed, skip the missed dose and administer the next dose on the regularly scheduled day.
In each case, patients can then resume their regular once-weekly dosing schedule.
Ozempic is available as single-patient-use injections, and there are multiple strength options:
0.25 mg or 0.5 mg dose pen (4 doses of 0.25 mg and 2 doses of 0.5 mg, or 4 doses of 0.5 mg)
1 mg dose pen (4 doses per pen)
2 mg dose pen (4 doses per pen)
Each Ozempic pen carton contains 4 NovoFine Plus needles with 1mg and 2mg pens and 6 NovoFine Plus needles with the 0.25/0.5mg dose pen.
Each injection is pre-filled and intended for use by one patient only.

Days 1 through 30: 1.5 mg orally once daily (this dose is not effective for glycemic control).
Escalation and Maintenance Ozempic Dosage:

Day 61 or thereafter if :
If no additional glycemic control is needed, then maintain the dosage at 4 mg orally once daily.

Week 5 to week 8: 0.5mg once a week

Adult weight reduction maintenance dose:
1.7 mg or 2.4 mg (recommended) injected subcutaneously once weekly.
Dose may be increased to 7.2 mg subcutaneously once weekly on patients who tolerate the 2.4 mg dosage for at least 4 weeks and additional weight reduction is clinically indicated.
Maximum dose 7.2 mg once weekly
Consider treatment response and tolerability when selecting the maintenance dosage
Pediatric patients' weight reduction maintenance dose (patients aged 12 years and older):
Either 2.4 mg (recommended) or 1.7 mg once weekly.
Consider treatment response and tolerability when selecting the maintenance dosage

Either 2.4 mg (recommended) or 1.7 mg once weekly, based on patient response and tolerance.
Non-cirrhotic metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH) with moderate to advanced liver fibrosis maintenance dose:
2.4 mg injected once weekly.
If a patient does not tolerate the 2.4 mg once-weekly maintenance dose, the dose may be reduced to 1.7 mg once weekly.
Re-escalation to 2.4 mg once weekly may be considered if the lower dose is tolerated.
In patients with type 2 diabetes, monitor blood glucose prior to starting Wegovy and during Wegovy treatment.
Wegovy Injections Strengths available:
Wegovy 0.25 mg pen delivers one 0.25 mg dose (0.25 mg/0.5 mL)
Wegovy 0.5 mg pen delivers one 0.5 mg dose (0.5 mg / 0.5 mL)
Wegovy 1 mg pen delivers one 1 mg dose (1 mg / 0.5 mL)

Titration: Follow the dosage escalation schedule, titrating every 30 days to achieve the maintenance dosage.

After 30 minutes of taking the tablet, you may eat, drink, or take other oral medicines.

Do not split, crush, or chew tablets.
Rybelsus Recommended Dosage R1 formulation
Start Rybelsus with 3 mg once daily for 30 days.
The 3 mg dose is intended for treatment initiation and is not effective for glycemic control.
After 30 days on the 3 mg dose, increase the dose to 7 mg once daily.
Dose may be increased to 14 mg once daily if additional glycemic control is needed after at least 30 days on the 7 mg dose.
Taking two 7 mg Rybelsus tablets to achieve a 14 mg dose is not recommended.
If a dose is missed, the missed dose should be skipped, and the next dose should be taken the following day.

Rybelsus Recommended Dosage R2 formulation
Start Rybelsus with 1.5 mg once daily for 30 days.

Switching Patients between Ozempic and Rybelsus
Patients treated with Rybelsus 14 mg daily can be transitioned to Ozempic subcutaneous injection 0.5 mg once weekly.
Patients can start Ozempic the day after their last dose of Rybelsus.
Patients treated with once-weekly Ozempic 0.5 mg subcutaneous injection can be transitioned to Rybelsus 7 mg or 14 mg.

Generic name: sertraline [ SER-tra-leen ] Brand name: Zoloft Dosage forms: tablet (100 mg; 25 mg; 50 mg), capsules (150 mg; 200 mg), oral solution (20 mg/mL) Drug class: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors
Medically reviewed by Melisa Puckey, BPharm .
Last updated on Sep 25, 2026.

Sertraline is a prescription medicine used to treat depression , obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), panic disorders , posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), social anxiety disorder , and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).
It is sold under the brand name Zoloft , and generic sertraline is widely available.
Sertraline belongs to a group of medicines called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors , or SSRIs.
It increases serotonin activity in the brain by blocking the reuptake of serotonin (a chemical messenger that nerve cells use to communicate) back into nerve cells, so more of it stays available.
Sertraline has only very weak effects on the reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine, and it does not block monoamine oxidase.
Sertraline is available as tablets (25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg), oral solution (20 mg/mL), and capsules (150 mg and 200 mg).
Sertraline is not a controlled substance.
Sertraline is FDA-approved to treat six conditions in adults:
Major depressive disorder (MDD) , the clinical term for depression.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) , where unwanted thoughts drive repeated behaviors.
Panic disorder , which causes sudden attacks of intense fear along with physical symptoms.
Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) , which can follow a frightening or traumatic event.
Social anxiety disorder (SAD) , also called social phobia.
Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) , a severe form of premenstrual symptoms.
In children and teenagers, sertraline is approved only for OCD, from age 6 upward.
Its safety and effectiveness have not been established in children under 6 years of age, or in children and teenagers for any condition other than OCD.
Not every sertraline product is approved for all six conditions:
Sertraline tablets and oral solution are approved for all of them.
Sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules are approved only for depression in adults and for OCD in adults and children aged 6 and over.

The most common sertraline side effects are nausea, diarrhea or loose stools, trouble sleeping, dry mouth, tiredness, dizziness, sleepiness, tremor, indigestion, agitation, reduced appetite, increased sweating, and sexual problems.
The table below shows how often each side effect was reported in pooled placebo-controlled trials in 3,066 adults, compared with 2,293 people taking placebo.
Some side effects were more common with particular conditions.

Sleepiness was more common in depression trials, insomnia and agitation in OCD trials, constipation and agitation in panic disorder trials, tiredness in PTSD trials, and insomnia, dizziness, tiredness, dry mouth, and a general feeling of being unwell in social anxiety disorder trials.
In PMDD trials, sleepiness, dry mouth, dizziness, tiredness, and stomach pain were more common.
In these trials, 12% of people taking sertraline stopped treatment because of a side effect, compared with 4% of people taking placebo.
The most common reasons for stopping were nausea (3%), diarrhea (2%), agitation (2%), and insomnia (2%).
SSRIs including sertraline can cause sexual problems.
In men, this can mean delayed ejaculation or being unable to ejaculate, lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection.
In women, it can mean lower sex drive and delayed orgasm or being unable to have an orgasm.
Changes in sex drive and sexual function can also be part of depression and anxiety themselves, so the timing of when symptoms started matters.
These numbers may underestimate how often sexual side effects happen, because people and their providers do not always raise the subject.
Tell your provider about any change in sexual function, since there may be ways to manage it.
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to sertraline: rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing.
Call your doctor at once if you have:

signs of serotonin syndrome , which can be life threatening: agitation, hallucinations, confusion, coma or other changes in mental state, a racing heartbeat, high or low blood pressure, dizziness, heavy sweating, fever, muscle stiffness, twitching or overactive reflexes, loss of coordination, seizures, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea;
unusual bleeding or bruising , including nosebleeds, bleeding gums, blood in vomit or stools, or black tarry stools;

signs of a manic episode : greatly increased energy, severe trouble sleeping, racing thoughts, reckless behavior, unusually grand ideas, excessive happiness or irritability, or talking more or faster than usual;
seizures or convulsions ;
eye pain, changes in vision, or swelling or redness in or around the eye , which can be signs of angle-closure glaucoma (a sudden rise in pressure inside the eye);
signs of low sodium in the blood (hyponatremia) : headache, trouble concentrating or thinking, memory problems, confusion, weakness, or feeling unsteady, which can lead to falls.
Severe cases have caused hallucinations, fainting, seizures, coma, and death;
fainting, chest discomfort, or an irregular heartbeat , which can be signs of a heart rhythm problem called QTc prolongation.

sentence: Reduced appetite and weight loss have been seen with SSRIs, so height and weight should be monitored during treatment.

Less common side effects reported during studies include tachycardia (fast heartbeat), tinnitus (ringing in the ears), underactive thyroid, enlarged pupils, blurred vision, blood in the stools, swelling, unsteady walking, irritability, fever, raised liver enzymes, anaphylaxis, diabetes, high cholesterol, low blood sugar, increased appetite, joint pain, muscle spasms, poor coordination, coma, convulsions, reduced alertness, numbness, lethargy, restlessness, fainting, aggression, teeth grinding, confusion, euphoric mood, hallucination, blood in the urine, milk production from the breasts, priapism (a long-lasting erection), vaginal bleeding, wheezing, yawning, hair loss, cold sweats, skin inflammation, blistering, itching, rash, hives, bleeding, high blood pressure, and flushing.

Side effects reported after sertraline came onto the market include increased clotting times, AV block, slow heartbeat, atrial arrhythmias, QTc prolongation, ventricular tachycardia including Torsade de Pointes, breast enlargement in men, raised prolactin, irregular periods, SIADH, blindness, optic neuritis, cataract, severe liver problems including hepatitis, jaundice, and liver failure with some fatal outcomes, pancreatitis, several blood disorders, angioedema, low sodium, high blood sugar, rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown), lockjaw, serotonin syndrome, movement disorders including akathisia and dystonia, psychosis, bedwetting, nightmares, sudden kidney failure, pulmonary hypertension, eosinophilic pneumonia, loss of smell, photosensitivity, severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, spasm of blood vessels in the brain, and vasculitis.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Do not take sertraline with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), or within 14 days of stopping one, because of the risk of serotonin syndrome.
This includes the antibiotic linezolid and intravenous methylene blue.
You also need to wait at least 14 days after stopping sertraline before starting an MAOI.
Do not take sertraline with pimozide, an antipsychotic medicine.
Do not take sertraline oral solution if you take disulfiram (Antabuse), because the solution contains alcohol.
Sertraline can raise the risk of bleeding, particularly if you also take aspirin, NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, other antiplatelet medicines, warfarin, or other anticoagulants.

Screening for a personal or family history of bipolar disorder, mania, or hypomania is recommended before starting sertraline, since treating a depressive episode with an antidepressant can trigger a manic episode in someone with bipolar disorder.
Do not stop taking sertraline suddenly.
Adverse reactions can occur when it is stopped, especially when it is stopped abruptly, so the dose should be lowered gradually where possible.
You should not take sertraline if you are allergic to sertraline or any of the ingredients in it, if you take an MAOI or have taken one in the past 14 days, or if you take pimozide.
Do not take the oral solution if you take disulfiram.
To make sure sertraline is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have or have ever had:
liver problems
kidney problems
heart problems, or risk factors for a heart rhythm problem called QTc prolongation
bipolar disorder or mania
seizures or convulsions
low sodium levels in your blood
bleeding problems, or you take a medicine that thins the blood
narrow angles in the eye or glaucoma
a stroke or high blood pressure
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, plan to become pregnant, or become pregnant while taking sertraline.
Studies of women exposed to sertraline in the first trimester suggest no overall difference in the risk of major birth defects compared with the background rate.
Some studies have reported increases in specific defects, but those results are inconclusive.

Taking sertraline late in pregnancy may raise the risk of newborn problems that need longer hospital stays, breathing support, and tube feeding, and of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), a serious lung problem.
Use in the month before delivery has been linked with a less than two-fold increase in the risk of postpartum hemorrhage (heavy bleeding after birth).
Stopping treatment is not automatically the safer choice.
In one study of 201 pregnant women with a history of major depression, those who stopped their antidepressant during pregnancy were more likely to relapse than those who continued.
This is a decision to make with your doctor.
Sertraline oral solution contains 12% alcohol and is not recommended during pregnancy, because there is no known safe level of alcohol exposure in pregnancy.
There is a pregnancy registry that collects information on antidepressant use in pregnancy.
You can join by calling 1-866-961-2388.
Low levels of sertraline and its breakdown products pass into breast milk.
In a pooled analysis of 53 mother and infant pairs, exclusively breastfed infants had an average of 2% of the sertraline levels measured in their mothers' blood, ranging from 0% to 15%.
No side effects were seen in those infants.
There is no information on whether sertraline affects milk production.
Talk with your doctor about the benefits of breastfeeding alongside your need for treatment.
Sertraline is approved for OCD in children aged 6 to 17 years.
It is not known to be safe and effective in children under 6, or for any other condition in this age group.

Children and teenagers taking sertraline should be monitored for worsening symptoms and suicidal thoughts, especially early in treatment and when the dose changes, and their weight and growth should be checked.
Older adults clear sertraline more slowly.
In one study, plasma clearance in people aged 65 and over was about 40% lower than in adults aged 25 to 32, so it took 2 to 3 weeks to reach steady levels rather than about 1 week.
Doctors usually start older adults at the low end of the dose range.
Older adults are also at greater risk of low sodium levels in the blood, particularly if they take diuretics (water pills) or are dehydrated.
Take sertraline exactly as prescribed, once a day, in either the morning or the evening.
Take it at around the same time each day.
Tablets and capsules can be taken with or without food.
Taking sertraline with food causes only a small increase in the amount absorbed.
Swallow capsules whole.
Do not open, crush, or chew them.
Your doctor may start you on a low dose and raise it gradually, usually no more often than once a week.
Keep taking sertraline even if you feel well, and do not stop without talking to your doctor first.
Tell any doctor or lab that you take sertraline before you have tests.
Sertraline can cause a false-positive result on urine screening tests for benzodiazepines, and this can continue for several days after you stop taking it.
A confirmatory test will tell the difference.
Store sertraline at room temperature, 68°F to 77°F (20°C to 25°C).

Rhabdomyolysis is a rare but serious side effect of statins, a class of cholesterol-lowering medications.
It involves the breakdown of muscle tissue, which releases substances into the bloodstream that can cause kidney damage.
While statins are generally safe, rhabdomyolysis from statins is uncommon and most likely to occur at high doses or when combined with certain other drugs.

Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic (water pill) used for heart failure, high blood pressure, fluid build-up (edema) caused by liver or kidney disease, and a hormone condition called primary hyperaldosteronism.
Spironolactone is sometimes prescribed off-label for women with acne or excessive facial hair growth (hirsutism).
Spironolactone works by blocking a hormone called aldosterone, which causes your body to pass more salt and water in your urine while keeping potassium in.
This is why it is called potassium-sparing, and it is what makes spironolactone different from most other water pills, which flush potassium out.
Spironolactone also blocks androgens such as testosterone from binding to the androgen receptor, which explains several of its side effects, including breast tenderness and breast growth.
Spironolactone is FDA-approved to treat adults with:
Heart failure (NYHA Class III-IV) with a reduced ejection fraction to help live longer, reduce swelling, and reduce the need for hospital stays.
It is taken alongside other heart failure medicines rather than on its own.
High blood pressure as an add-on treatment for people whose blood pressure is not controlled well enough by other medicines.
Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of stroke and heart attack.

Fluid build-up (edema ) caused by cirrhosis of the liver when cutting back on fluid and salt has not been enough, and also for swelling caused by nephrotic syndrome (a kidney disorder) when treating the underlying disease and using other water pills have not worked well enough.
Primary hyperaldosteronism, which is a condition where the adrenal glands make too much aldosterone.
Spironolactone is used short-term to prepare for surgery, and long-term for people who are not suitable for surgery.
Spironolactone tablets come in 25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg strengths.
Spironolactone 25 mg is the strength most often used to start treatment.
There is also a banana-flavored oral liquid for people who cannot swallow tablets.
The liquid and the tablets are not interchangeable, so never switch between them without your doctor changing your dose.

Reported spironolactone side effects include breast and nipple pain in both men and women, a lower sex drive, trouble getting or keeping an erection, irregular or missed periods, bleeding after menopause, dizziness, headache, drowsiness, feeling sluggish, leg cramps, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach cramps, indigestion, hair thinning, and itching.
The most common side effect of spironolactone is breast growth in men, known as gynecomastia.
In the main heart failure study, about 9 in 100 men taking an average of 26 mg a day developed it.
The chance goes up on higher doses.
It can start anywhere from one or two months into treatment to more than a year later, and it usually goes away after the medicine is stopped.
Several of these effects are dose-related, so they are more likely on higher doses, and many settle after the dose is lowered or the medicine is stopped.
How often most of them happen is not known, because they come from reports gathered after the medicine was approved rather than from counted numbers in trials.
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to spironolactone: hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:

signs of a high potassium level (hyperkalemia), such as muscle weakness or a heavy feeling in your legs, a slow or uneven heartbeat, numbness or tingling in your hands, feet, or lips, nausea, or feeling restless and on edge;
a light-headed feeling like you might pass out, which can be a sign you have low blood pressure (hypotension)
little or no urination, or swelling in your ankles, hands, or feet, which can be signs your kidneys are struggling (worsening renal function);
signs of a low sodium level, such as confusion, severe weakness, muscle pain or cramps, feeling unsteady, or slurred speech;
severe or ongoing vomiting or diarrhea, since losing too much fluid and salt can send your blood pressure and kidney function the wrong way;
a skin rash that spreads or blisters, peeling skin, sores in your mouth, or a rash with a fever and swollen glands, which can be signs of a rare but serious skin reaction;
yellowing of your eyes or skin, dark urine, or pain in your upper stomach, which can be signs of a liver problem;
a fever, sore throat, or unusual bruising or bleeding, which can be signs of a problem with your blood cells; or
new confusion, unsteadiness, or extreme drowsiness if you have liver disease, since spironolactone can make brain function worse in people with cirrhosis.
Men are most likely to notice effects linked to spironolactone blocking male hormones.
These include breast growth and breast tenderness, a lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection.
Breast growth is dose related, so tell your doctor early rather than waiting, since a lower dose or a different medicine may be an option.
Women may notice irregular periods, missed periods, breast tenderness, or bleeding after menopause.
Some women also notice patchy darkening of the skin on the face.
Report any unexpected bleeding after menopause to your doctor so it can be checked properly rather than assumed to be a side effect.
The main long-term concerns with spironolactone are chemical rather than something you would feel.
Over time it can push your potassium too high, and it can also lower your sodium, magnesium, and calcium, raise your blood sugar, and raise your uric acid, which occasionally brings on gout .
This is why you need regular blood tests for as long as you take it, not just at the start.
In animal studies, spironolactone given at high doses over long periods caused tumors in rats, mainly in hormone-producing glands and the liver.
No increase in tumors was seen at the lower doses tested, which were still around five times the highest recommended human dose when adjusted for body size.
Whether this happens in people is not known.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Do not take spironolactone if you have a high potassium level in your blood, if you have Addison's disease (an adrenal gland disorder), or if you are taking eplerenone (Inspra), another medicine of the same type.
Spironolactone can raise your potassium to a dangerous level.
A high potassium level can cause a life-threatening change in your heart rhythm, and it often causes no symptoms until it is already high.
Your doctor should check your potassium with a blood test within a week of you starting spironolactone or having your dose changed, and regularly after that.

Your risk of high potassium is greater if your kidneys do not work well, if you take potassium supplements or a salt substitute containing potassium, or if you take an ACE inhibitor, an ARB, an NSAID, heparin, or trimethoprim.
Do not use potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium unless your doctor has specifically told you to.
Passing too much fluid can drop your blood pressure and make your kidney function worse, especially if you are also taking an ACE inhibitor or an ARB.
Tell your doctor if you feel faint, or if you become unwell with vomiting or diarrhea.
If you have cirrhosis with fluid in your abdomen, spironolactone is usually started in hospital, because sudden shifts in fluid and salt can affect how your brain works.
Spironolactone should be avoided in pregnancy where possible, because it blocks male hormones and may affect how a male baby develops.
You should not use spironolactone if you are allergic to it, or if you have:
a high level of potassium in your blood (hyperkalemia);
Addison's disease (an adrenal gland disorder); or
if you are taking eplerenone.
To make sure spironolactone is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have or have ever had:
kidney disease, or reduced kidney function;
liver disease, especially cirrhosis or fluid in the abdomen (ascites);
an electrolyte imbalance, such as a low sodium, magnesium, or calcium level;
dehydration, or any illness causing vomiting or diarrhea;
diabetes, since spironolactone can raise blood sugar;
gout or a high uric acid level; or
prostate cancer treated with abiraterone.
Spironolactone blocks the effect of male hormones, and male hormones are needed for a male baby to develop normally.
In animal studies, male offspring exposed in the womb showed feminized development.
The limited information available in humans has not shown a clear increase in birth defects, but the concern remains.
Your doctor will usually avoid spironolactone in pregnancy, or talk through the possible risk to a male baby with you.
Untreated heart failure, cirrhosis, and high blood pressure also carry real risks in pregnancy, so this is a decision to make with your doctor rather than by stopping on your own.
Spironolactone itself does not pass into breast milk.
Its active breakdown product, canrenone, has been found in breast milk in very small amounts that are not expected to affect a breastfed baby.
No side effects were reported in the one infant studied over a short period, and the long-term picture is not known.
Talk to your doctor so you can weigh this up together.
Spironolactone has not been shown to be safe and effective in children.
The oral liquid is specifically not recommended for treating high blood pressure in children, because of the hormonal effects of the medicine.
Any use in a child must be decided and monitored by a specialist.
Spironolactone is cleared by the kidneys, and kidney function tends to fall with age.
Older adults are therefore more likely to build up a high potassium level, so kidney function and potassium need monitoring.
Take spironolactone exactly as prescribed.
