Yes.
Spironolactone is a diuretic, or water pill, and it belongs to the group called potassium-sparing diuretics.
It works by blocking aldosterone, a hormone that makes your kidneys hold onto salt and water.
Unlike most water pills, which make you lose potassium, spironolactone makes your body keep potassium in.
It is a weaker diuretic than medicines such as furosemide, which is one reason it is often given alongside another water pill rather than instead of one.
Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating acne, but doctors sometimes prescribe it off-label for hormonal acne in women.
Off-label means a doctor is prescribing a medicine for something other than its approved uses, which is legal and common, but it means the FDA has not reviewed the medicine for that purpose.
The reason it is used this way relates to how spironolactone works.
As well as blocking aldosterone, spironolactone attaches to the androgen receptor, the docking point for male hormones such as testosterone.
Male hormones increase how much oil the skin produces, and oil production is one factor in acne.
Because acne is not an approved use, there is no FDA-approved dose for it.
Any dose is chosen by the prescriber.

Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy because it may affect how a male baby develops, which is an important consideration for anyone taking it for a skin condition rather than a heart or kidney condition.

If you are considering spironolactone for acne, this is a conversation to have with a doctor or dermatologist who can review your full medical history, since spironolactone still carries the same risk of raising your potassium level, whatever it is prescribed for.
Weight gain is not a recognized side effect of spironolactone, and it is not listed in the medicine's official prescribing information.
Spironolactone is a diuretic, so it usually causes a small drop in weight in the first week or two as your body sheds extra fluid.
If you are gaining weight while taking it, it is worth telling your doctor rather than assuming the medicine is to blame.
Rapid weight gain with swelling in your ankles or legs or shortness of breath can be a sign of fluid building up, which may mean the condition being treated needs a closer look.
Slower weight gain is more often down to appetite, activity, or another medicine.
Hair thinning, known as alopecia, is listed as a possible side effect of spironolactone, though how often it happens is not known.
It is reported far less often than breast tenderness or breast growth.
The picture is complicated because spironolactone is also prescribed off label for hair loss in women, on the basis that blocking male hormones may help with hormone-related thinning.
Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating hair loss.
If your hair is thinning while you take it, speak to your doctor, since there are several possible causes worth ruling out.

Tamsulosin is used to treat the symptoms of an enlarged prostate, also called benign prostatic hyperplasia or BPH .

These symptoms include a weak urine stream, trouble starting to urinate, dribbling, a feeling of not emptying the bladder completely, needing to urinate often or urgently, and getting up at night to urinate.
Tamsulosin belongs to a group of medicines called alpha blockers.
It works by blocking alpha-1 receptors in the prostate and bladder neck.
Blocking these receptors relaxes the muscle there, which improves urine flow and eases BPH symptoms.
Tamsulosin is taken once daily, about half an hour after the same meal each day.
Capsules should be swallowed whole and not crushed, chewed, or opened.
The tamsulosin brand name was Flomax, which has now been discontinued in the U.S., but generic tamsulosin is available.
Tamsulosin is not approved to treat high blood pressure, and it is not approved for use in women or children.
Do not take tamsulosin if you are allergic to tamsulosin or to any of the ingredients in the capsule.
Do not take tamsulosin with other alpha blockers such as alfuzosin (Uroxatral), doxazosin (Cardura), prazosin (Minipress), silodosin (Rapaflo), or terazosin (Hytrin).
Do not take tamsulosin 0.4 mg with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole.
These medicines raise tamsulosin levels in your blood.
Tamsulosin can lower your blood pressure when you stand up, which may make you feel dizzy or faint.
This is most likely when you first start taking it, when your dose changes, or when you start it again after a break.
Get up slowly from sitting or lying down.
Be careful driving or doing anything that needs you to be alert until you know how tamsulosin affects you.
In rare cases (probably fewer than 1 in 50,000 patients), tamsulosin can cause priapism, a painful erection that lasts a long time and is not related to sexual activity.
Get medical help straight away if this happens, because without prompt treatment it can lead to permanent erectile dysfunction.
An enlarged prostate and prostate cancer can occur together.
Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before you start tamsulosin and at regular intervals while you are taking it.
Tamsulosin can cause a problem called intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) during cataract or glaucoma surgery.
Tell your eye surgeon that you take tamsulosin or have taken it in the past, even if you stopped months ago.
Do not stop taking tamsulosin before surgery unless your surgeon tells you to.
If you are already booked in for cataract or glaucoma surgery, starting tamsulosin is not recommended.
If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, talk to your doctor before starting again.
You will need to restart at the 0.4 mg dose.
Many other medicines can interact with tamsulosin.
Tell your doctor about everything you take, including prescription medicines, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
To make sure tamsulosin is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
an allergy to tamsulosin or any of its ingredients
an allergy to sulfa drugs
kidney problems
liver problems
low blood pressure (hypotension)
Also tell your doctor if you are planning to have cataract or glaucoma surgery.
Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before starting tamsulosin and at regular intervals afterwards.
Tamsulosin is not approved for use in women or in children.
Take tamsulosin exactly as prescribed.
Follow the directions on your prescription label and read any medication guides or instruction sheets.
Take once a day, about 30 minutes after the same meal each day.
For example, 30 minutes after dinner.
Swallow the capsule whole.
Do not crush, chew, break, or open it.
If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, do not start again without talking to your doctor.

Tirzepatide is a once-weekly injection available as two brands: Zepbound (for weight loss, weight management, and obstructive sleep apnea) and Mounjaro (for type 2 diabetes and to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in those with type 2 diabetes at high risk).
Zepbound (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for weight loss and weight management in adults with obesity, or in overweight adults with at least one weight-related medical condition.
Zepbound is also approved to treat moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults with obesity.
Mounjaro (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes in adults and children aged 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar (glucose) levels, used alongside diet and exercise.

It is also approved to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke) in adults with type 2 diabetes who are at high risk for these events.
Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/ GLP-1 receptor agonist , meaning it activates two gut hormone receptors that help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar.
It works by reducing appetite, increasing feelings of fullness, slowing gastric emptying, boosting insulin release when blood sugar is high, and reducing glucagon secretion.
Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe, and should always be used together with diet and exercise.
Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes.
It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.

The most common tirzepatide side effects are:
Diarrhea
Vomiting
Constipation
Nausea (mild to moderate)
Decreased appetite
Abdominal pain.
Tirzepatide can cause serious side effects.
Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following:

Severe stomach pain (pancreatitis): Stop taking tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider immediately if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting, or pain that spreads to your back.
Kidney problems: Diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting can cause dehydration, which may lead to kidney problems.
Drink plenty of fluids to reduce this risk and tell your doctor if you are unable to keep fluids down.
Gallbladder problems: Symptoms include severe upper stomach pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or clay-colored stools.

Serious allergic reactions: Seek emergency medical attention if you experience hives, difficulty breathing, feeling light-headed, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (anaphylaxis or angioedema).
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): Symptoms may include headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery.
Vision changes: Tell your doctor about any blurred vision or other vision changes, particularly if you have type 2 diabetes.
Thyroid tumor: Symptoms may include a lump or swelling in your neck, trouble swallowing, hoarseness, or shortness of breath.
Mental health changes: Tell your healthcare provider right away about any new or worsening depression, mood changes, or thoughts of suicide or self-harm.
Aspiration during surgery: Tirzepatide slows stomach emptying, which may increase the risk of food or liquid entering the lungs during procedures using anesthesia or sedation.
Tell all your healthcare providers you are taking tirzepatide before any planned surgery or procedure.
This is not a complete list of side effects.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects, or report them to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Who should not use tirzepatide:
Type 1 diabetes patients (tirzepatide is not approved for type 1 diabetes)
Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC)
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).
Use with Caution:
History of pancreatitis (safety not established in patients with prior pancreatitis)
Severe gastrointestinal disease
Diabetic retinopathy complications.
Tirzepatide carries a Boxed Warning for the risk of possible thyroid tumors.
Tell your healthcare provider if you get a lump or swelling in your neck, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or shortness of breath.
These may be symptoms of thyroid cancer.
In studies with rats, tirzepatide and medicines that work like tirzepatide have caused thyroid tumors, including thyroid cancer.
It is not known if tirzepatide will cause thyroid tumors, or a type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) in people.

Do not use tirzepatide if you or any of your family have ever had a type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), or if you have an endocrine system condition called Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).
Tell your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to tirzepatide, any other medications, or any of the ingredients in this medicine.
There is a list of ingredients in this medicine, at the bottom of this page.
Tell your healthcare team if you are planning surgery or other procedure that uses anesthesia or deep sedation.
Tell your doctor if you have or have ever had kidney or pancreas disease, a history of diabetic retinopathy or any stomach problems such as difficulty digesting food.
Tell your doctor if you plan to become pregnant, are pregnant, or are breastfeeding.
If you become pregnant while taking this medicine, you should tell your doctor.
There is a pregnancy exposure registry for women who take Zepbound during pregnancy.
Talk to your healthcare provider about how you can take part, call 1-844-524-0039, or visit https://pregnancyregistry.lilly.com/zepbound.

You should follow the directions on your prescription label carefully and ask your pharmacist or doctor to explain any part you do not understand.
It is important to use this medicine exactly as directed.
Do not take more or less of it or take it more often than prescribed by your doctor.
Tirzepatide is injected under the skin (subcutaneously) using a pre-filled single-dose pen, a multi-dose KwikPen (for single patient use), and a single-dose vial with a syringe.
Caregivers or patients should be trained on proper injection techniques and should read the instructions for use .
Children should not inject themselves with the KwikPen; an adult caregiver should give a child their injections.
Tirzepatide is usually given:
once a week.
can be given with or without meals at any time of the day.
may be injected into the thigh, abdomen, or have another person inject it into the back of your upper arm
You should rotate injection sites with each dose.
Do not inject into a muscle (intramuscularly) or vein (intravenously).
Do not mix insulin and tirzepatide together in the same injection.
You may give an injection of tirzepatide and insulin in the same body area, but not right next to each other.
Your doctor will probably start you on a low dose, which may be gradually increased, but not more than once every 4 weeks.
You may change the day of the week you use tirzepatide as long as there are at least three days between doses.
Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor.
The KwikPen contains 4 fixed doses, and one dose is injected weekly (subcutaneously).
For your weekly dose, you need to turn the dose knob all the way until it stops AND the 1 icon is in the dose window.
After 4 doses, throw away (discard) the Pen, including the unused medicine.
The Pen will prevent you from dialing a full dose after you have given yourself 4 weekly doses.
Do not inject the leftover medicine.
Do not transfer the leftover medicine from your Pen into a syringe.
Do not share your tirzepatide Pen with other people, even if the pen needle has been changed.
You may give other people a serious infection or get a serious infection from them.
People who are blind or have vision problems should not use the Pen without help from a person who has been trained to use the pen.

Single-dose pens and vials (Zepbound and Mounjaro)
Store in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C).
Do not freeze.
Do not use if the medication has been frozen.
Keep in the original carton until use to protect from light.
If needed, single-dose pens and vials may be kept at room temperature up to 86°F (30°C) for up to 21 days.
Once at room temperature, do not return to the refrigerator.
Discard after 21 days at room temperature if unused.
KwikPen (Zepbound KwikPen and Mounjaro KwikPen)
Before first use:
Store in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C).
Keep until the expiration date printed on the label.
Do not freeze.
Discard the pen if it has been frozen.
After first use:
Store in the refrigerator or at room temperature up to 86°F (30°C).
Keep away from heat and light.
Discard the pen 30 days after first use, even if medicine remains.
Discard after 4 weekly doses have been given.
General storage advice (all tirzepatide products)
Keep all pens, vials, needles, and syringes out of reach of children.
Dispose of used pens, needles, and syringes in an approved sharps container.

The most effective GLP-1 drug for weight loss currently (as of early 2026) is tirzepatide, marketed under the names Zepbound (for weight loss) and Mounjaro (for diabetes).
Clinical trials and recent meta-analyses consistently show tirzepatide delivers the most substantial weight reduction among GLP-1 medications, with average losses of up to 22.5% of body weight.

Mounjaro (generic name: tirzepatide) will start to lower your blood sugar levels right away but it can take 8 to 12 weeks to reach your target A1C goal.
When compared to some other diabetes treatments, studies have shown that it can take 8 weeks to reach an A1C target of ≤7% and 12 weeks to reach an A1C ≤6.5% with Mounjaro.
Significant weight loss can occur as early as 28-weeks.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are prescription medicines used for type 2 diabetes and long-term weight management.
Semaglutide products include Ozempic, Rybelsus, Wegovy, and Wegovy HD, while tirzepatide products include Mounjaro and Zepbound.
These medicines differ in dosing, approved uses, side effects, and cost, so discuss options with your healthcare provider.

Tramadol is an opioid agonist that may be used to treat moderate to moderately severe chronic pain in adults, when other pain treatments such as non-opioid pain medicines do not treat your pain well enough, or you cannot tolerate them.
Extended-release forms of tramadol may be used in adults who require around-the-clock treatment of their pain for an extended period.
An opioid pain medicine such as tramadol can put you at risk for overdose and death.
Even if you take your dose correctly as prescribed, you are at risk for opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse that can lead to death.
Brands of tramadol include ConZip, Qdolo, Ryzolt, Ultram, Ultram ER, and Ultracet.
Many have been discontinued, but generic tramadol is still available .

Taking tramadol in combination with other pain-relieving medicines such as acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or aspirin can provide better pain relief than just taking one pain-relieving medicine by itself (see Can you take tramadol in combination with acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or aspirin? )
Tramadol first gained FDA approval on March 3, 1995.
Originally, it was classified as a non-controlled substance, but it was reclassified in 2014 to Schedule IV of the Controlled Substances Act with restrictions on its prescribing .
Tramadol is an opioid (see Is tramadol an opioid?
A person's genetics can affect the pain-relieving properties of tramadol (see How do genetics affect tramadol?
Tramadol is used for the management of moderate to moderately severe pain in adults, including postoperative pain (pain after surgery).
Tramadol treats pain severe enough to require opioids and may be used as an alternative to other forms of pain relief that did not relieve pain well enough or were not tolerated.
Tramadol extended-release capsules may be used by adults who require around-the-clock treatment of their moderate to moderately severe chronic pain for an extended time.

Tramadol should not be used in children younger than 12 years old, or anyone younger than 18 years old with other risk factors (such as breathing problems), or who have recently had surgery to remove their tonsils or adenoids.
Extended-release tramadol (Ultram ER) should not be given to anyone younger than 18 years.
Yes, tramadol is an opioid.
The opioid activity of tramadol is due to its binding to mu-opioid receptors.
Get emergency help or call 911 right away if you take too many tramadol (overdose).
When you first start taking tramadol, when your dose is changed, or if you take too much (overdose), serious or life-threatening breathing problems that can lead to death may occur.
Ask your healthcare provider about medicines like naloxone or nalmefene that can be used in an emergency to reverse an opioid overdose.

Taking tramadol with other opioid medicines , benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids (gabapentin or pregabalin), alcohol, or other central nervous system depressants (including street drugs) can cause severe drowsiness, decreased awareness, breathing problems, coma, and death.
Do not take tramadol with any other medicine that contains tramadol .
Check the label of every pain medicine you take, as some combination products contain tramadol.
You should be given a Medication Guide each time you fill a tramadol prescription .
Read it every time, even if you have taken tramadol before, because the information may have changed.
Your healthcare provider or pharmacist should also go through the risks of tramadol and how to take it safely with you, and explain what to do in an emergency.
Never give anyone else your tramadol .
They could die from taking it.
Selling or giving away tramadol is against the law.
Store tramadol securely , out of sight and reach of children, and in a location not accessible by others, including visitors to the home.

dizziness or vertigo
nausea
constipation

drowsiness
vomiting
itching.
Dry mouth is also commonly reported with the extended-release forms of tramadol.

Immediate-release formulations (tablets and oral solution)
Treatment usually starts at 25 mg a day, increasing by 25 mg every 3 days to reach 100 mg a day (25 mg four times a day).
Doses of 25 mg are measured using the oral solution, as immediate-release tramadol tablets are only available as 50 mg.
For the immediate-release tablets, a common starting dose is one 50 mg tablet a day to see how well you tolerate it, or the dose prescribed by your doctor.
If needed, the total daily dose can then be increased by 50 mg every 3 days as tolerated, to reach 200 mg a day (one 50 mg tablet four times a day).
After this titration, 50 mg to 100 mg (one or two 50 mg tablets) can be taken every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain.
The maximum is 400 mg a day: eight 50 mg tablets in divided doses, or 80 mL of the 5 mg/mL oral solution.
Extended-release capsules and tablets
Tramadol ER 100 mg once a day (one 100 mg tablet or capsule) at approximately the same time each day.
Can be increased by 100 mg every 5 days if needed, to a maximum of 300 mg a day, taken as one dose once a day.
Extended-release tramadol is not intended for as-needed pain relief, and should not be taken with any other tramadol product.
Dosage in kidney or liver impairment
Severe kidney impairment: for immediate-release tramadol, doses are spaced 12 hours apart, and the maximum is 200 mg a day (four 50 mg tablets, given as two 100 mg doses 12 hours apart).
Severe liver impairment: for immediate-release tramadol, the recommended dose is 50 mg (one 50 mg tablet) every 12 hours, which is 100 mg a day.
Extended-release tramadol is not recommended for people with severe kidney or severe liver impairment.
Dosage in older adults

No separate maximum dose applies on the basis of age, but tramadol should be started at the low end of the dosing range and increased slowly, with frequent review for drowsiness and breathing problems.
Side effects that led people to stop treatment were more common over the age of 75, mostly stomach and bowel effects, such as constipation.
Kidney function also tends to decline with age, which affects how tramadol is cleared, so your doctor may take this into account when choosing your dose.
